Lack of labelled datasets for antibodies compared to general proteins, which prevents automated feature identification and annotation.
TopK SAEs may not consistently generate monosemantic features for all concepts.
future_direction: Conduct exhaustive steering analyses to quantitatively measure the steerability of Top-K and Ordered SAE features.
Scale SAE training using more expansive, annotated datasets like FLAb to enable models to identify domain-specific abstractions.
Use SAEs to generate antibody libraries with properties such as developability and specificity.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a mechanistic interpretability technique that have been used to provide insight into learned concepts within large protein language models. Here, we employ TopK and Ordered SAEs to investigate an autoregressive antibody language model, p-IgGen, and steer its generation. We show that TopK SAEs can reveal biologically meaningful latent features, but high feature concept correlation does not guarantee causal control over generation. In contrast, Ordered SAEs impose an hierarchical structure that reliably identifies steerable features, but at the expense of more complex and less interpretable activation patterns. These findings advance the mechanistic interpretability of domain-specific protein language models and suggest that, while TopK SAEs are sufficient for mapping latent features to concepts, Ordered SAEs are preferable when precise generative steering is required.

papers.title: The Local Interaction Basis: Identifying Computationally-Relevant and Sparsely Interacting Features in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can the Local Interaction Basis (LIB) method find interpretable and sparsely-interacting features in neural networks, particularly in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Local Interaction Basis (LIB), a method to transform neural network activations into a basis of computationally-relevant and sparsely-interacting features, and shows it works on toy models but not on language models.
papers.conclusion: LIB is promising on toy models but does not achieve interpretable and sparsely-interacting features on language models, likely due to the assumption of a linear non-overcomplete basis.
papers.key_findings:
LIB identifies more computationally-relevant features than PCA in modular addition and CIFAR-10 models.
LIB features interact more sparsely than PCA features in CIFAR-10 and some layers of language models.
LIB does not produce more interpretable features than PCA in language models.
Integrated gradient interaction graphs can aid circuit discovery in toy models.
LIB does not reveal modular structure in language models.
papers.limitation: LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models.
future_direction: Generalizing LIB to overcomplete bases to handle features in superposition.
Exploring other ways to average attributions over the dataset.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the behavior of neural networks by reverse-engineering their internal computations. However, current methods struggle to find clear interpretations of neural network activations because a decomposition of activations into computational features is missing. Individual neurons or model components do not cleanly correspond to distinct features or functions. We present a novel interpretability method that aims to overcome this limitation by transforming the activations of the network into a new basis - the Local Interaction Basis (LIB). LIB aims to identify computational features by removing irrelevant activations and interactions. Our method drops irrelevant activation directions and aligns the basis with the singular vectors of the Jacobian matrix between adjacent layers. It also scales features based on their importance for downstream computation, producing an interaction graph that shows all computationally-relevant features and interactions in a model. We evaluate the effectiveness of LIB on modular addition and CIFAR-10 models, finding that it identifies more computationally-relevant features that interact more sparsely, compared to principal component analysis. However, LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models. We conclude that LIB is a promising theory-driven approach for analyzing neural networks, but in its current form is not applicable to large language models.

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Language Models Are Specific to Human Language
papers.research_question: Are correlations between language model hidden states and fMRI brain responses robust to dimensionality concerns, and are they specific to models trained on human language and dependent on positional encoding?
papers.core_contribution: The study confirms that correlations between transformer language model hidden states and human brain activity during language tasks are robust, specific to language-trained models, and heavily dependent on positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: The internal representations of transformer language models are strongly correlated with human brain activity during language processing, and this alignment is specific to language-trained models and relies on positional information.
papers.key_findings:
Removing positional encodings significantly reduces brain-model correlations and distorts the geometric similarity between model and brain representational spaces.
Dimensionality reduction via PCA does not eliminate the correlations, indicating they are not an artifact of the curse of dimensionality.
Models trained on non-linguistic data (protein sequences) show negligible alignment with brain activity, confirming the language-specificity of the effects.
Causal (decoder-only) language models show higher alignment with brain activity than bidirectional models.
The geometric structure of model and brain representations, measured by CKA and Gromov-Wasserstein distance, is similar and degrades when positional information is removed.
papers.limitation:
The dataset includes only 243 stimuli and 6 subjects, limiting statistical power and generalizability.
The head-wise analysis pooled voxels across cortical regions without distinguishing between different regions of interest.
The study uses text-only models and fMRI data from reading tasks; future work should use modality-matched datasets (e.g., audio models with spoken language tasks).
future_direction: Increase the number of subjects and model diversity to improve statistical power and generalizability.
Conduct finer-grained region-of-interest (ROI) by head analysis to reveal differential alignment patterns.
Use modality-matched datasets (e.g., spoken-language tasks with audio models) to disentangle task effects from representational differences.
papers.abstract: Previous work has shown correlations between the hidden states of large language models and fMRI brain responses, on language tasks. These correlations have been taken as evidence of the representational similarity of these models and brain states. This study tests whether these previous results are robust to several possible concerns. Specifically this study shows: (i) that the previous results are still found after dimensionality reduction, and thus are not attributable to the curse of dimensionality; (ii) that previous results are confirmed when using new measures of similarity; (iii) that correlations between brain representations and those from models are specific to models trained on human language; and (iv) that the results are dependent on the presence of positional encoding in the models. These results confirm and strengthen the results of previous research and contribute to the debate on the biological plausibility and interpretability of state-of-the-art large language models.

papers.title: Using attribution to decode binding mechanism in neural network models for chemistry
papers.research_question: Why do virtual screening models make the predictions they do? The paper aims to assess the influence of dataset biases on the prediction of protein binding.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework that uses attribution methods (Integrated Gradients) to test hypotheses about binding logic and reveal dataset bias in neural network models for chemistry, showing that models can achieve perfect accuracy while learning spurious correlations.
papers.conclusion: Attribution methods can reveal dataset bias in neural network models for chemistry, and models can be fooled by adversarial examples despite perfect accuracy. Practitioners should analyze model predictions and not rely solely on aggregate accuracy metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on synthetic binding logics achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test sets but often have low attribution-AUC, indicating they learn spurious correlations.
Attribution methods (Integrated Gradients) can be used to identify dataset biases and construct adversarial examples that fool the model.
The attribution-AUC metric quantifies how well the model's attributions align with the hypothesized binding logic.
In the ADRB2 dataset, the model achieves perfect accuracy but very low attribution-AUC, indicating it does not learn the correct binding logic.
The framework provides a test for dataset bias given a hypothesis, indicating when models must be simplified/regularized or datasets augmented.
papers.limitation: Attributions offer a reductive view of the model's internal logic and fail to capture higher-order feature interactions.
future_direction: Further research to reveal feature interactions in the model's predictions.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracy at classifying molecules with respect to whether they bind to specific protein targets. A key breakthrough would occur if these models could reveal the fragment pharmacophores that are causally involved in binding. Extracting chemical details of binding from the networks could enable scientific discoveries about the mechanisms of drug actions. However, doing so requires shining light into the black box that is the trained neural network model, a task that has proved difficult across many domains. Here we show how the binding mechanism learned by deep neural network models can be interrogated, using a recently described attribution method. We first work with carefully constructed synthetic datasets, in which the molecular features responsible for "binding" are fully known. We find that networks that achieve perfect accuracy on held-out test datasets still learn spurious correlations, and we are able to exploit this nonrobustness to construct adversarial examples that fool the model. This makes these models unreliable for accurately revealing information about the mechanisms of protein-ligand binding. In light of our findings, we prescribe a test that checks whether a hypothesized mechanism can be learned. If the test fails, it indicates that the model must be simplified or regularized and/or that the training dataset requires augmentation.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Interpretable Structure in Small Gene Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders extract biologically meaningful representations from small gene language models?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract biologically meaningful representations from small gene language models, revealing features like nucleotide identity and transcription factor binding motifs, demonstrating that compact models learn structured genomic representations.
papers.conclusion: SAEs can extract biologically meaningful representations from small gene language models, highlighting their ability to capture essential genomic features.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs extracted sparse features corresponding to individual nucleotides with high precision.
SAEs identified features aligned with known transcription factor binding motifs, such as MA1596.1 and MA0052.5.
Even compact models effectively capture transcription factor binding specificity.
The recall variability indicates the complexity and redundancy of regulatory elements in genomic sequences.
future_direction: Extend SAE approach to other genomic contexts like non-coding regions or species-specific variations.
Explore SAEs for model refinement and interpretability across different architectures.
Apply SAEs to other biological modalities like single-cell gene expression and multi-omics datasets.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs), revealing latent latent features with semantical meaning. This interpretability has also proven valuable in biological domains: applying SAEs to protein language models uncovered meaningful features related to protein structure and function. More recently, SAEs have been used to analyze genomics-focused models such as Evo 2, identifying interpretable features in gene sequences. However, it remains unclear whether SAEs can extract meaningful representations from small gene language models, which have fewer parameters and potentially less expressive capacity. To address it, we propose applying SAEs to the activations of a small gene language model. We demonstrate that even small-scale models encode biologically relevant genomic features, such as transcription factor binding motifs, that SAEs can effectively uncover. Our findings suggest that compact gene language models are capable of learning structured genomic representations, and that SAEs offer a scalable approach for interpreting gene models across various model sizes.

papers.title: MolReasoner: Toward Effective and Interpretable Reasoning for Molecular LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across various domains, but their ability to perform molecular reasoning remains underexplored. Existing methods mostly rely on general-purpose prompting, which lacks domain-specific molecular semantics, or fine-tuning, which faces challenges in interpretability and reasoning depth, often leading to structural and textual hallucinations. To address these issues, we introduce MolReasoner, a two-stage framework that transitions LLMs from memorization to high-fidelity chemical reasoning. In the Mol-SFT stage, knowledge-enhanced Chain-of-Thought (CoT) data provides a strong foundation, while the Mol-RL stage refines reasoning using a novel, task-adaptive reward system to mitigate hallucinations. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that MolReasoner significantly outperforms a wide range of strong baselines in both molecule generation and captioning tasks. Further analyses highlight the framework's synergistic design and its ability to produce more interpretable outputs. Our work presents a principled and effective new approach for advancing high-fidelity molecular reasoning.

papers.title: Sparse Modular Activation for Efficient Sequence Modeling
papers.research_question: Can neural networks learn to activate their attention modules on demand to achieve better quality-efficiency trade-off? How much extra attention is needed for the SSMs on a task-by-task basis?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Modular Activation (SMA), a general mechanism for sparsely and dynamically activating sub-modules in neural networks, and applies it to design SeqBoat, a novel hybrid SSM-GAU architecture that achieves significantly better quality-efficiency trade-offs in sequence modeling.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Modular Activation (SMA) enables efficient and interpretable dynamic module activation, and its application in SeqBoat demonstrates superior quality-efficiency trade-offs across diverse sequence modeling tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SeqBoat achieves new state-of-the-art average accuracy among linear-complexity hybrid models on the Long Range Arena (LRA) benchmark.
SeqBoat provides substantial training speedup and memory reduction compared to Transformer and other baselines, e.g., 10.4x speedup and 95% memory reduction on the LRA Text task.
The learned sparse activation patterns of the GAU module directly reveal the amount of attention needed for each task and data sample.
The working memory mechanism in SeqBoat enables linear inference complexity with theoretically infinite attention span and outperforms chunking-based models.
SeqBoat achieves competitive performance on speech classification (Speech Commands) and language modeling (enwik8) with improved efficiency.
papers.limitation:
The current implementation of SMA is I/O bounded due to copying large tensors with scatter operations, and no custom fused kernels were used for memory bandwidth optimization.
Experiments were limited to models of moderate size due to computational resource constraints, leaving scalability to larger models uncertain.
future_direction: Explore the scaling behavior of SMA and how to incorporate it with pre-trained large language models.
Investigate the interpretability of module activation patterns and their correlation with input tokens or model predictions.
Scale up SMA with a large number of modules, potentially impacting Mixture-of-Experts research.
papers.abstract: Recent hybrid models combining Linear State Space Models (SSMs) with self-attention mechanisms have demonstrated impressive results across a range of sequence modeling tasks. However, current approaches apply attention modules statically and uniformly to all elements in the input sequences, leading to sub-optimal quality-efficiency trade-offs. To address this limitation, we introduce Sparse Modular Activation (SMA), a general mechanism enabling neural networks to sparsely and dynamically activate sub-modules for sequence elements in a differentiable manner. Through allowing each element to skip non-activated sub-modules, SMA reduces computation and memory consumption of neural networks at both training and inference stages. To validate the effectiveness of SMA on sequence modeling, we design a novel neural architecture, SeqBoat, which employs SMA to sparsely activate a Gated Attention Unit (GAU) based on the state representations learned from an SSM. By constraining the GAU to only conduct local attention on the activated inputs, SeqBoat can achieve linear inference complexity with theoretically infinite attention span, and provide substantially better quality-efficiency trade-off than the chunking-based models. With experiments on a wide range of tasks, including long sequence modeling, speech classification and language modeling, SeqBoat brings new state-of-the-art results among hybrid models with linear complexity, and reveals the amount of attention needed for each task through the learned sparse activation patterns. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/renll/SeqBoat.

papers.title: Partial Symmetry Enforced Attention Decomposition (PSEAD): A Group-Theoretic Framework for Equivariant Transformers in Biological Systems
papers.research_question: How can local, partial, and approximate symmetries inherent in biological data be embedded into Transformer self-attention to improve generalization, interpretability, and computational efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Partial Symmetry Enforced Attention Decomposition (PSEAD) framework, a group-theoretic method that decomposes Transformer self-attention into orthogonal irreducible components aligned with local symmetry subgroups, enabling models to learn and exploit partial symmetries in biological data.
papers.conclusion: PSEAD offers a principled paradigm for advancing machine learning in biology by embedding symmetry-aware inductive biases into Transformers, leading to more performant and insightful AI systems for understanding biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
The self-attention mechanism is inherently equivariant under local permutation group actions, allowing for a principled decomposition into symmetry-specific components.
PSEAD is expected to improve generalization to novel motifs with similar partial symmetries, enhance interpretability via symmetry-channel analysis, and increase computational efficiency by focusing on relevant symmetric subspaces.
The framework can be extended to dynamic biological processes in reinforcement learning, such as protein folding and drug discovery.
papers.limitation:
The framework currently focuses on finite permutation groups and requires specifying the target symmetry group a priori; it does not automatically learn or infer symmetries from data.
Real biological symmetries are often approximate due to noise, mutations, or conformational flexibility, and the framework's robustness to such approximations requires further research.
future_direction: Extension to continuous symmetry groups (e.g., SO(3), SE(3)) using harmonic analysis.
Development of multi-resolution equivariant models that integrate symmetries across different scales.
Adaptive symmetry detection to learn relevant local symmetry groups from data without prior specification.
Integration with causal inference to identify causal relationships via symmetry-disentangled features.
Enhanced robustness to approximate symmetries through soft projection or statistical modeling.
Optimized computational implementations for large-scale biological datasets.
papers.abstract: This research introduces the Theory of Partial Symmetry Enforced Attention Decomposition (PSEAD), a new and rigorous group-theoretic framework designed to seamlessly integrate local symmetry awareness into the core architecture of self-attention mechanisms within Transformer models. We formalize the concept of local permutation subgroup actions on windows of biological data, proving that under such actions, the attention mechanism naturally decomposes into a direct sum of orthogonal irreducible components. Critically, these components are intrinsically aligned with the irreducible representations of the acting permutation subgroup, thereby providing a powerful mathematical basis for disentangling symmetric and asymmetric features. We show that PSEAD offers substantial advantages. These include enhanced generalization capabilities to novel biological motifs exhibiting similar partial symmetries, unprecedented interpretability by allowing direct visualization and analysis of attention contributions from different symmetry channels, and significant computational efficiency gains by focusing representational capacity on relevant symmetric subspaces. Beyond static data analysis, we extend PSEAD's applicability to dynamic biological processes within reinforcement learning paradigms, showcasing its potential to accelerate the discovery and optimization of biologically meaningful policies in complex environments like protein folding and drug discovery. This work lays the groundwork for a new generation of biologically informed, symmetry-aware artificial intelligence models.

papers.title: Multi-scale Graph Autoregressive Modeling: Molecular Property Prediction via Next Token Prediction
papers.research_question: How can we bridge the gap between graph topology preservation and scalable autoregressive training to enable decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via next-token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Connection-Aware Motif Sequencing (CamS), a graph-to-sequence representation that enables decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via next-token prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance on molecular property prediction benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CamS bridges the gap between graph topology and autoregressive training, enabling effective molecular property prediction via next-token prediction with a standard decoder-only Transformer backbone.
papers.key_findings:
CamS-LLaMA achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoleculeNet and MoleculeACE benchmarks.
Multi-scale concatenation is the key driver of performance.
The causal serialization effectively drives attention toward cliff-determining structural differences.
CamS provides a more nuanced structural discrimination than descriptor-based approaches like KPGT.
The method combines general-purpose robustness with fine-grained structural discriminability.
papers.limitation: Vocabulary materialization involves expensive subgraph-isomorphism matching that prohibits direct training on billion-scale corpora.
papers.abstract: We present Connection-Aware Motif Sequencing (CamS), a graph-to-sequence representation that enables decoder-only Transformers to learn molecular graphs via standard next-token prediction (NTP). For molecular property prediction, SMILES-based NTP scales well but lacks explicit topology, whereas graph-native masked modeling captures connectivity but risks disrupting the pivotal chemical details (e.g., activity cliffs). CamS bridges this gap by serializing molecular graphs into structure-rich causal sequences. CamS first mines data-driven connection-aware motifs. It then serializes motifs via scaffold-rooted breadth-first search (BFS) to establish a stable core-to-periphery order. Crucially, CamS enables hierarchical modeling by concatenating sequences from fine to coarse motif scales, allowing the model to condition global scaffolds on dense, uncorrupted local structural evidence. We instantiate CamS-LLaMA by pre-training a vanilla LLaMA backbone on CamS sequences. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on MoleculeNet and the activity-cliff benchmark MoleculeACE, outperforming both SMILES-based language models and strong graph baselines. Interpretability analysis confirms that our multi-scale causal serialization effectively drives attention toward cliff-determining differences.

papers.title: Associative memory inspires improvements for in-context learning using a novel attention residual stream architecture
papers.research_question: How can insights from associative memory models be used to improve in-context learning (ICL) in Transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory, that allows information to flow directly between attention heads, leading to faster and improved in-context learning in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: The residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory models, improves in-context learning in Transformers and shows promising scalability to larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
A one-layer associative memory model (AMICL) can perform in-context learning on a classification task.
Adding a residual stream for attention values (and to a lesser extent, queries) in a two-layer Transformer speeds up the emergence of ICL during training compared to a classic Transformer.
Naively applying the residual value stream architecture to small language models (8M and 1B parameters) trained on Tiny Stories indicates performance improvements scale to larger models and more naturalistic data.
future_direction: Testing the residual attention stream architecture on larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the interpretability of the residual stream for understanding model mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive ability to utilise information within the context of their input sequences to appropriately respond to data unseen by the LLM during its training procedure. This ability is known as in-context learning (ICL). Humans and non-human animals demonstrate similar abilities, however their neural architectures differ substantially from LLMs. Despite this, a critical component within LLMs, the attention mechanism, resembles modern associative memory models, widely used in and influenced by the computational neuroscience community to model biological memory systems. Using this connection, we introduce an associative memory model capable of performing ICL. We use this as inspiration for a novel residual stream architecture which allows information to directly flow between attention heads. We test this architecture during training within a two-layer Transformer and show its ICL abilities manifest more quickly than without this modification. We then apply our architecture in small language models with 8 million and 1 billion parameters, focusing on attention head values, with results also indicating improved performance at these larger and more naturalistic scales.

papers.title: Systematic Evaluation of Single-Cell Foundation Model Interpretability Reveals Attention Captures Co-Expression Rather Than Unique Regulatory Signal
papers.research_question: Does attention in single-cell foundation models capture causal regulatory relationships or just co-expression? Do attention-derived edge scores provide incremental value beyond gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models encode structured biological information (e.g., protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers) but do not capture causal regulatory signal; they provide no incremental value over gene-level features for predicting perturbation outcomes.
papers.conclusion: Attention patterns in single-cell foundation models capture co-expression rather than causal regulatory signal, and the proposed evaluation framework provides a reusable quality-control standard for mechanistic interpretability in this domain.
papers.key_findings:
Attention patterns show layer-specific biological specialization but do not outperform trivial gene-level baselines for perturbation prediction.
Pairwise edge scores (attention or correlation) provide no incremental predictive value beyond gene-level features.
Causal ablation of 'regulatory' attention heads does not degrade perturbation prediction, indicating distributed redundancy.
The relationship between attention and correlation is context-dependent across cell types and perturbation modalities.
Cell-State Stratified Interpretability (CSSI) improves attention-derived GRN recovery by controlling for heterogeneity.
papers.limitation:
Causal ablation only performed on Geneformer V2-316M, not on scGPT due to architectural differences.
Perturbation data limited to four cell types and two modalities; additional tissues, species, and architectures remain untested.
No decisive positive control demonstrates recovery of known causal regulatory structure in a realistic perturbation setting.
future_direction: Test additional tissues, species, and architectures (e.g., scFoundation).
Focus interpretability efforts on residual-stream geometry, MLP-stored knowledge, or representations from the full forward pass.
papers.abstract: We present a systematic evaluation framework - thirty-seven analyses, 153 statistical tests, four cell types, two perturbation modalities - for assessing mechanistic interpretability in single-cell foundation models. Applying this framework to scGPT and Geneformer, we find that attention patterns encode structured biological information with layer-specific organisation - protein-protein interactions in early layers, transcriptional regulation in late layers - but this structure provides no incremental value for perturbation prediction: trivial gene-level baselines outperform both attention and correlation edges (AUROC 0.81-0.88 versus 0.70), pairwise edge scores add zero predictive contribution, and causal ablation of regulatory heads produces no degradation. These findings generalise from K562 to RPE1 cells; the attention-correlation relationship is context-dependent, but gene-level dominance is universal. Cell-State Stratified Interpretability (CSSI) addresses an attention-specific scaling failure, improving GRN recovery up to 1.85x. The framework establishes reusable quality-control standards for the field.

papers.title: Beyond Converging Representations A Philosophical Response on the Interpretation Risks of Scientific Foundation Models
papers.research_question: Do scientific foundation models of different modalities, architectures, and training data learn similar internal representations of matter?
papers.core_contribution: Representations learned by nearly sixty scientific foundation models across string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities are highly aligned, and they converge as model performance improves, suggesting a common underlying representation of physical reality.
papers.conclusion: Representational alignment serves as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models, and current models remain limited by training data and inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on different input modalities (e.g., string encodings and 3D coordinates) show significant representational alignment.
As models improve in energy prediction performance, their representations converge towards those of the best-performing models.
Local (CKNNA) and global (dCor) alignment metrics show consistent trends, indicating robust representational similarity.
Intrinsic dimensionality (Id) of embeddings is consistent across models for a given dataset, suggesting a universal low-dimensional structure.
For in-distribution data, high-performing models align closely while weak models diverge; for out-of-distribution data, most models collapse to a low-information representation.
papers.limitation: Today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure.
future_direction: Using representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models.
Tracking the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale.
Selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.
papers.abstract: Machine learning models of vastly different modalities and architectures are being trained to predict the behavior of molecules, materials, and proteins. However, it remains unclear whether they learn similar internal representations of matter. Understanding their latent structure is essential for building scientific foundation models that generalize reliably beyond their training domains. Although representational convergence has been observed in language and vision, its counterpart in the sciences has not been systematically explored. Here, we show that representations learned by nearly sixty scientific models, spanning string-, graph-, 3D atomistic, and protein-based modalities, are highly aligned across a wide range of chemical systems. Models trained on different datasets have highly similar representations of small molecules, and machine learning interatomic potentials converge in representation space as they improve in performance, suggesting that foundation models learn a common underlying representation of physical reality. We then show two distinct regimes of scientific models: on inputs similar to those seen during training, high-performing models align closely and weak models diverge into local sub-optima in representation space; on vastly different structures from those seen during training, nearly all models collapse onto a low-information representation, indicating that today's models remain limited by training data and inductive bias and do not yet encode truly universal structure. Our findings establish representational alignment as a quantitative benchmark for foundation-level generality in scientific models. More broadly, our work can track the emergence of universal representations of matter as models scale, and for selecting and distilling models whose learned representations transfer best across modalities, domains of matter, and scientific tasks.

papers.title: Integrating Evolutionary and Compositional Features with ML and DL for Robust and Interpretable Druggable Protein Prediction
papers.research_question: How can evolutionary and compositional features be integrated with machine learning and deep learning for robust and interpretable druggable protein prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a hybrid feature representation combining Average Block-based PSSM and Dipeptide Composition for druggable protein prediction, achieving high accuracy with statistical validation and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The hybrid feature representation enables strong predictive performance for druggable protein prediction, with SVM and CapsBiLSTM achieving high accuracy and AUC scores, validated statistically, and providing interpretable insights into sequence descriptors.
papers.key_findings:
Hybrid features (AB-PSSM + DPC) significantly outperform individual descriptors in predicting druggable proteins.
SVM and CapsBiLSTM models achieve classification accuracies above 90% and ROC-AUC/PR-AUC scores above 95%.
Statistical tests (DeLong's test, McNemar's test, bootstrap confidence intervals) confirm the robustness and significance of the improvements.
Interpretability analyses using SHAP and t-SNE reveal biologically significant sequence descriptors influencing druggability.
The proposed framework outperforms existing machine learning and ensemble-based methods in accuracy and interpretability.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Druggable proteins are essential targets in contemporary therapeutic discovery, and their precise identification is necessary for the progression of rational drug design. Traditional biochemical screening techniques are costly, laborious, and protracted, whereas current computational models typically attain only moderate efficacy and seldom offer robust statistical validation or biological interpretability. To mitigate these limitations, we offer a hybrid computational approach that amalgamates evolutionary and compositional information by merging Average Block-based Position-Specific Scoring Matrix (AB-PSSM) characteristics with Dipeptide Composition (DPC) into a 600-dimensional representation. The hybrid feature space was assessed utilizing three machine learning algorithms (support vector machine, random forest, and XGBoost) alongside three deep learning architectures (CapsBiLSTM, ResCapsNetPlus, and ResNet1D) following a rigorous five-fold out-of-fold cross-validation protocol to guarantee fairness and reproducibility. A thorough assessment revealed that the hybrid attributes significantly surpassed individual descriptors, with the SVM and CapsBiLSTM classifiers attaining classification accuracies of 90% and ROC-AUC and PR-AUC values surpassing 95%. The robustness and reliability were further validated by statistical analyses, including DeLong’s test, McNemar’s test, and bootstrap confidence intervals, demonstrating that the observed enhancements were substantial and consistent. Furthermore, interpretability investigations employing SHAP feature attribution and t-SNE visualization underscored biologically significant sequence descriptors as pivotal factors influencing druggability, thus mitigating the "black box" constraint inherent in numerous deep learning methodologies. This study presents a statistically validated, interpretable, and high-performing framework for predicting druggable proteins, which outperforms current machine learning and ensemble-based methods, establishing a clear basis for future applications in precision medicine and drug discovery.

papers.title: Superior Molecular Representations from Intermediate Encoder Layers
papers.research_question: Are we overlooking superior molecular representations by adhering to the final-layer convention in chemistry? Specifically, do intermediate layers of molecular encoders provide more informative and task-relevant features for downstream property prediction than the final layer?
papers.core_contribution: Intermediate layers of pretrained molecular encoders retain more general-purpose features and yield superior performance on downstream property prediction tasks compared to the final layer, both when used as frozen embeddings and when finetuned, leading to substantial performance improvements and computational efficiency.
papers.conclusion: The common practice of relying solely on final-layer representations from pretrained molecular encoders is suboptimal; exploring intermediate layers yields substantial performance gains and computational savings, advocating for a shift beyond the final-layer default.
papers.key_findings:
Using frozen embeddings from optimal intermediate layers improves downstream performance by an average of 5.4% (up to 28.6%) compared to the final-layer, with 81% of model-task combinations preferring a non-final layer.
Finetuning encoders truncated at intermediate depths achieves average improvements of 8.5% (up to 40.8%) over finetuning the complete encoder, with 71% of cases showing gains.
Label-free probes (tokenized-molecule entropy and adjacent-layer CKA) show that final layers undergo specialization and compression, while intermediate layers retain more transferable features.
The optimal intermediate layer varies by encoder architecture and downstream task; no single depth is universally best.
Frozen embedding performance correlates with finetuning performance (median Pearson correlation 0.60), providing an efficient proxy for selecting layers to finetune.
papers.limitation: The study is constrained by computational resources to five encoders and 22 ADMET tasks; extending the analysis to a broader set of molecular encoders and chemical domains could further validate the findings.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to a broader set of molecular encoders and chemical domains.
Conduct future work with additional architectures, multiple random seeds, and more exhaustive hyperparameter searches for deeper insights and more robust generalizations.
papers.abstract: Pretrained molecular encoders have become indispensable in computational chemistry for tasks such as property prediction and molecular generation. However, the standard practice of relying solely on final-layer embeddings for downstream tasks may discard valuable information. In this work, we first analyze the information flow in five diverse molecular encoders and find that intermediate layers retain more general-purpose features, whereas the final-layer specializes and compresses information. We then perform an empirical layer-wise evaluation across 22 property prediction tasks. We find that using frozen embeddings from optimal intermediate layers improves downstream performance by an average of 5.4%, up to 28.6%, compared to the final-layer. Furthermore, finetuning encoders truncated at intermediate depths achieves even greater average improvements of 8.5%, with increases as high as 40.8%, obtaining new state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. These findings highlight the importance of exploring the full representational depth of molecular encoders to achieve substantial performance improvements and computational efficiency. The code will be made publicly available.

papers.title: Mode-locking Theory for Long-Range Interaction in Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What is the underlying mechanism of long-range interaction in artificial neural networks for visual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the mode-locking theory as the underlying mechanism for visual long-range interaction in artificial neural networks and validates it through simulation and real-world task experiments.
papers.conclusion: The mode-locking theory explains the formation of lateral inhibition structures in artificial neural networks, and incorporating this principle can enhance model robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Mode-locking interference patterns emerge in CNN models (LongNet) trained for long-range interaction simulation.
The Transformer-based skeleton detection model (SkeSwin) exhibits feature maps that resemble the mode-locking pattern and the lateral inhibition principle of the human visual cortex.
Incorporating long-range image information in the detection model enhances robustness, as demonstrated by SkeSwin's performance on skeleton detection datasets.
The mode-locking pattern is observed across various network architectures, backbones, initialization methods, and label settings in the simulation experiment.
The proposed theory aligns with the lateral interaction principle (intermediate excitation and lateral inhibition) observed in the visual cortex.
future_direction: Using the mode-locking theory to improve the long-range interaction ability of CNN models for more powerful global modeling and robust, efficient calculation.
Further exploration of the theory's potential practical applications in tasks like object detection, pose estimation, and skeleton detection.
papers.abstract: Visual long-range interaction refers to modeling dependencies between distant feature points or blocks within an image, which can significantly enhance the model's robustness. Both CNN and Transformer can establish long-range interactions through layering and patch calculations. However, the underlying mechanism of long-range interaction in visual space remains unclear. We propose the mode-locking theory as the underlying mechanism, which constrains the phase and wavelength relationship between waves to achieve mode-locked interference waveform. We verify this theory through simulation experiments and demonstrate the mode-locking pattern in real-world scene models. Our proposed theory of long-range interaction provides a comprehensive understanding of the mechanism behind this phenomenon in artificial neural networks. This theory can inspire the integration of the mode-locking pattern into models to enhance their robustness.

papers.title: Task-Level Insights from Eigenvalues across Sequence Models
papers.research_question: How do eigenvalue spectra of sequence models, analyzed through a dynamical systems framework, relate to their memory retention and selectivity in different tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that eigenvalue spectra of sequence models, when viewed through a dynamical systems framework, reveal characteristic patterns related to memory retention and selectivity, and these patterns correlate with task requirements and model performance.
papers.conclusion: Eigenvalue analysis can serve as a systematic method for understanding the capabilities of sequence models on a given task, opening up new possibilities for initialization schemes and architectural design choices that encourage spectral properties well-suited to particular tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Eigenvalue distributions show a concentration near one when long-term memory is important, and near zero when selective memory is required.
Architectural modifications (like adding gating or convolution) shift the eigenvalue spectra in predictable ways and affect performance accordingly.
Attention models tend to have eigenvalues both near zero and above one, which may lead to gating behavior and instability.
LTI SSMs (like S4) tend to have eigenvalues concentrated near one, which is good for long-term memory but not for selective tasks.
Mamba-2, as an LPV SSM, shows a balance between memory and selectivity, leading to competitive performance across tasks.
papers.limitation: The analysis focuses on eigenvalue magnitudes in predefined bins and may not capture the full complexity of model dynamics; other components of the models also shape their behavior.
future_direction: Extending the analyses to capture the full complexity of model dynamics, as well as other architectural choices such as positional embeddings.
papers.abstract: Although softmax attention drives state-of-the-art performance for sequence models, its quadratic complexity limits scalability, motivating linear alternatives such as state space models (SSMs). While these alternatives improve efficiency, their fundamental differences in information processing remain poorly understood. In this work, we leverage the recently proposed dynamical systems framework to represent softmax, norm and linear attention as dynamical systems, enabling a structured comparison with SSMs by analyzing their respective eigenvalue spectra. Since eigenvalues capture essential aspects of dynamical system behavior, we conduct an extensive empirical analysis across diverse sequence models and benchmarks. We first show that eigenvalues influence essential aspects of memory and long-range dependency modeling, revealing spectral signatures that align with task requirements. Building on these insights, we then investigate how architectural modifications in sequence models impact both eigenvalue spectra and task performance. This correspondence further strengthens the position of eigenvalue analysis as a principled metric for interpreting, understanding, and ultimately improving the capabilities of sequence models.

papers.title: Characterizing Large Language Model Geometry Helps Solve Toxicity Detection and Generation
papers.research_question: What are the geometric properties of LLMs that best characterize the representations of a given prompt and generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric characterization of LLMs (MHA and MLP) that enables principled methods for bypassing RLHF protection and for toxicity detection using unsupervised features.
papers.conclusion: Geometric characterization of LLMs provides both theoretical insights and practical tools for safer AI, enabling the detection of toxic inputs and generations and exposing weaknesses in current RLHF methods.
papers.key_findings:
The output of the Multi-Head Attention (MHA) mapping lives in the Minkowski sum of convex hulls of embedded tokens, and its intrinsic dimension can be controlled via prompt manipulation.
Increasing the intrinsic dimension of the MHA embedding through informed prompt manipulation can bypass RLHF safeguards and induce toxic generation.
The MLP partitions the manifold induced by the MHA, and its expressivity grows exponentially with the MHA's intrinsic dimension.
A small set of unsupervised geometric features (spline features) extracted from pre-trained LLMs can effectively solve toxicity detection and domain classification tasks.
The proposed features achieve state-of-the-art performance on toxicity detection benchmarks with low latency and without requiring model fine-tuning.
papers.limitation: The proposed features perform aggressive dimensionality reduction and are likely most suited for coarse-grained tasks (such as toxicity and domain detection); finer-grained statistics may be required for other downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) drive current AI breakthroughs despite very little being known about their internal representations. In this work, we propose to shed the light on LLMs inner mechanisms through the lens of geometry. In particular, we develop in closed form $(i)$ the intrinsic dimension in which the Multi-Head Attention embeddings are constrained to exist and $(ii)$ the partition and per-region affine mappings of the feedforward (MLP) network of LLMs' layers. Our theoretical findings further enable the design of novel principled solutions applicable to state-of-the-art LLMs. First, we show that, through our geometric understanding, we can bypass LLMs' RLHF protection by controlling the embedding's intrinsic dimension through informed prompt manipulation. Second, we derive interpretable geometrical features that can be extracted from any (pre-trained) LLM, providing a rich abstract representation of their inputs. We observe that these features are sufficient to help solve toxicity detection, and even allow the identification of various types of toxicity. Our results demonstrate how, even in large-scale regimes, exact theoretical results can answer practical questions in LLMs. Code: https://github.com/RandallBalestriero/SplineLLM

papers.title: The Molecular Structure of Thought: Mapping the Topology of Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models learn and represent effective Long Chain-of-Thought?
papers.core_contribution: The paper models Long Chain-of-Thought as a molecular structure with three bond types and introduces Mole-Syn, a method to synthesize effective Long CoT structures, improving performance and RL stability.
papers.conclusion: The molecular structure view explains how LLMs learn Long CoT, and Mole-Syn enables effective synthesis of these structures for improved reasoning performance.
papers.key_findings:
Long CoT reasoning exhibits stable molecular-like structures formed by deep-reasoning, self-reflection, and self-exploration bonds.
Semantic isomers with compatible bond structures are crucial for effective Long CoT learning, while incompatible structures lead to instability.
Distillation from strong reasoning LLMs successfully imparts Long CoT structures, but distillation from weak instruction LLMs or human traces fails.
Mole-Syn can synthesize effective Long CoT structures by transferring behavior distributions, boosting performance across benchmarks.
Conflict between two stable molecular structures during training causes structural chaos and degrades performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often fail to learn effective long chain-of-thought (Long CoT) reasoning from human or non-Long-CoT LLMs imitation. To understand this, we propose that effective and learnable Long CoT trajectories feature stable molecular-like structures in unified view, which are formed by three interaction types: Deep-Reasoning (covalent-like), Self-Reflection (hydrogen-bond-like), and Self-Exploration (van der Waals-like). Analysis of distilled trajectories reveals these structures emerge from Long CoT fine-tuning, not keyword imitation. We introduce Effective Semantic Isomers and show that only bonds promoting fast entropy convergence support stable Long CoT learning, while structural competition impairs training. Drawing on these findings, we present Mole-Syn, a distribution-transfer-graph method that guides synthesis of effective Long CoT structures, boosting performance and RL stability across benchmarks.

papers.title: Site-Net: Using global self-attention and real-space supercells to capture long-range interactions in crystal structures
papers.research_question: How can global self-attention and real-space supercells be used to capture long-range interactions in crystal structures for property prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Site-Net is a transformer architecture that uses global self-attention and real-space supercells to capture long-range interactions in crystal structures, achieving state-of-the-art performance on band gap prediction.
papers.conclusion: Site-Net effectively captures long-range interactions in crystal structures and achieves competitive performance on band gap prediction, with potential for improvement via more extensive hyperparameter tuning and the use of larger supercells.
papers.key_findings:
Site-Net achieves a mean absolute error of 0.251 eV on the Matbench band gap regression task, demonstrating competitive performance.
Attention heads in Site-Net become specialized to deal with primarily short- or long-range interactions.
Enforcing a distance cutoff limit of 5 Å on the attention decreases model performance, confirming that longer-range interactions meaningfully contribute to predictions.
Site-Net learns from interactions beyond the nearest neighbor atomic sites.
The model performance is consistent across band gap values.
papers.limitation:
The model is computationally intensive and has a quadratic dependence on the number of atoms in the crystal in terms of VRAM and computational load.
The hyperparameter search was only preliminary, and the hyperparameters used are likely far from optimal.
The cutoff limit of 100 atoms excludes about 3% of crystal structures in the dataset during training due to memory constraints.
Model performance may be limited by the size of the supercell and could improve with larger supercells.
future_direction: More extensive hyperparameter tuning.
Using larger supercells to improve performance.
Applying the method to disordered crystal structures.
papers.abstract: Site-Net is a transformer architecture that models the periodic crystal structures of inorganic materials as a labelled point set of atoms and relies entirely on global self-attention and geometric information to guide learning. Site-Net processes standard crystallographic information files to generate a large real-space supercell, and the importance of interactions between all atomic sites is flexibly learned by the model for the prediction task presented. The attention mechanism is probed to reveal Site-Net can learn long-range interactions in crystal structures, and that specific attention heads become specialized to deal with primarily short- or long-range interactions. We perform a preliminary hyperparameter search and train Site-Net using a single graphics processing unit (GPU), and show Site-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance on a standard band gap regression task.

papers.title: Maximum entropy methods for extracting the learned features of deep neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we interpret deep neural networks and extract the features they learn from input data using maximum entropy methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a maximum entropy method for interpreting deep neural networks by sampling sequences that preserve penultimate layer activations, allowing extraction of learned features such as motifs and nucleosome positioning signals.
papers.conclusion: The maximum entropy method provides a valuable tool for interpreting deep neural networks, particularly in biological sequence analysis, and demonstrates synergy between statistical physics and machine learning for extracting subtle sequence features.
papers.key_findings:
The MaxEnt method successfully captures XOR logic learned by a simple ANN, while Saliency Map and DeepLIFT methods fail to do so.
The MaxEnt method localizes CTCF binding motifs with better agreement with conventional motif discovery tools (MEME/FIMO) than Saliency Map and DeepLIFT.
The MaxEnt method extracts nucleosome positioning signals, including periodic GC content at 10 bp intervals, more effectively than Saliency Map and DeepLIFT.
The method can assess the importance of global sequence features (e.g., GC content) via a feature importance score derived from the variance of MCMC samples.
Features extracted by MaxEnt (low-variance principal components) can be used for classification, as demonstrated by a nearest neighbor classifier achieving 76% accuracy.
papers.limitation: The MaxEnt method is computationally expensive compared to Saliency Map and DeepLIFT due to MCMC sampling.
papers.abstract: New architectures of multilayer artificial neural networks and new methods for training them are rapidly revolutionizing the application of machine learning in diverse fields, including business, social science, physical sciences, and biology. Interpreting deep neural networks, however, currently remains elusive, and a critical challenge lies in understanding which meaningful features a network is actually learning. We present a general method for interpreting deep neural networks and extracting network-learned features from input data. We describe our algorithm in the context of biological sequence analysis. Our approach, based on ideas from statistical physics, samples from the maximum entropy distribution over possible sequences, anchored at an input sequence and subject to constraints implied by the empirical function learned by a network. Using our framework, we demonstrate that local transcription factor binding motifs can be identified from a network trained on ChIP-seq data and that nucleosome positioning signals are indeed learned by a network trained on chemical cleavage nucleosome maps. Imposing a further constraint on the maximum entropy distribution also allows us to probe whether a network is learning global sequence features, such as the high GC content in nucleosome-rich regions. This work thus provides valuable mathematical tools for interpreting and extracting learned features from feed-forward neural networks.

papers.title: On the token distance modeling ability of higher RoPE attention dimension
papers.research_question: How do different dimensions in Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) contribute to modeling token distances and long-range dependencies in attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that higher dimensions in RoPE attention heads correlate with longer token distances and identifies 'Positional Heads' with strong distance-dimension correlation that are crucial for long-text comprehension.
papers.conclusion: Higher dimensions in RoPE are more effective at distinguishing token distances, and Positional Heads with correlated dimension allocation are crucial for integrating information across distances in long-text tasks, providing insights for future research.
papers.key_findings:
In most attention heads, higher-dimensional low-frequency components contribute more to attention scores than lower-dimensional high-frequency components.
Input lengths exceeding the pre-training length cause anomalies in high-dimensional components, and length extrapolation extends the high-dimensional attention allocation for longer token distances.
Attention heads with strong correlation between token distance and dimension allocation, termed 'Positional Heads', are key for modeling text distances.
Ablation of Positional Heads significantly reduces model performance on long-context tasks such as question answering and code completion.
The Spearman correlation coefficient can effectively identify Positional Heads based on their distance-dimension correlation.
papers.limitation:
The dimensional decomposition approach is based on the explicit meaning of dimensions in rotary position embeddings and is not applicable to all types of position encodings.
Computational resource constraints limited validation with longer input sequences and analysis of fine-tuning impacts on these attention heads.
future_direction: Leverage the properties of Positional Heads to address challenging tasks such as long text comprehension.
Conduct more detailed experimental analysis with longer input sequences and fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Length extrapolation algorithms based on Rotary position embedding (RoPE) have shown promising results in extending the context length of language models. However, understanding how position embedding can capture longer-range contextual information remains elusive. Based on the intuition that different dimensions correspond to different frequency of changes in RoPE encoding, we conducted a dimension-level analysis to investigate the correlation between a hidden dimension of an attention head and its contribution to capturing long-distance dependencies. Using our correlation metric, we identified a particular type of attention heads, which we named Positional Heads, from various length-extrapolated models. These heads exhibit a strong focus on long-range information interaction and play a pivotal role in long input processing, as evidence by our ablation. We further demonstrate the correlation between the efficiency of length extrapolation and the extension of the high-dimensional attention allocation of these heads. The identification of Positional Heads provides insights for future research in long-text comprehension.

papers.title: BERT Learns (and Teaches) Chemistry
papers.research_question: Can attention mechanisms in BERT be used to identify important molecular substructures (functional groups) from SMILES string representations and apply these learned representations to chemical property prediction tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that BERT's attention mechanisms can identify chemically relevant functional groups from SMILES strings without domain heuristics, and that these learned representations can be applied to downstream chemical property prediction tasks.
papers.conclusion: Attention visualization in BERT provides a data-driven method to identify functional groups and important molecular substructures from SMILES strings, offering a potentially useful tool for computational chemistry despite not achieving state-of-the-art performance on downstream tasks.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's attention heads, trained only on SMILES strings, learn to attend to atoms that correspond to known active reaction sites (functional groups) in molecules, even without explicit reaction data.
When fine-tuned on chemical property regression tasks (e.g., solubility), specific attention heads in BERT focus on relevant substructures (e.g., carbon chains for solubility).
Using BERT embeddings as features for graph models (GCN, GAT) on toxicity prediction tasks yields competitive but not state-of-the-art performance compared to canonical atom featurization.
Attention visualization of BERT trained on chemical data can serve as a tool for chemistry practitioners to quickly identify important substructures related to various chemical properties.
papers.limitation:
BERT embeddings did not improve upon the state of the art when used as features for graph models on toxicity prediction; the learned information appears to be a subset of that captured by canonical atom featurization.
Some molecules in the Tox21 dataset contain atoms not present in BERT's vocabulary, which may detract from performance.
Attention heads after fine-tuning on most chemical property tasks (QED, SAS) showed little change from pretraining, except for the solubility task, suggesting the fine-tuning may find a local optimum close to pretraining weights.
future_direction: Using a larger dataset of 96 million molecules from PubMed to train BERT, given that language models thrive with abundant data.
Designing a loss function that penalizes distances between embeddings of different SMILES strings representing the same molecule to force BERT to learn the inherent graphical meaning.
Further investigating the approach of analyzing chemical property-bearing molecular substructures via fine-tuning to make it a more useful tool for chemists.
papers.abstract: Modern computational organic chemistry is becoming increasingly data-driven. There remain a large number of important unsolved problems in this area such as product prediction given reactants, drug discovery, and metric-optimized molecule synthesis, but efforts to solve these problems using machine learning have also increased in recent years. In this work, we propose the use of attention to study functional groups and other property-impacting molecular substructures from a data-driven perspective, using a transformer-based model (BERT) on datasets of string representations of molecules and analyzing the behavior of its attention heads. We then apply the representations of functional groups and atoms learned by the model to tackle problems of toxicity, solubility, drug-likeness, and synthesis accessibility on smaller datasets using the learned representations as features for graph convolution and attention models on the graph structure of molecules, as well as fine-tuning of BERT. Finally, we propose the use of attention visualization as a helpful tool for chemistry practitioners and students to quickly identify important substructures in various chemical properties.

papers.title: Probing Graph Representations
papers.research_question: What is encoded in the representations learned by graph-based models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a probing framework to analyze graph representations and shows that transformer-based graph models capture more chemically relevant information compared to message-passing GNNs.
papers.conclusion: Probing is a useful diagnostic tool for understanding and evaluating graph-based models, especially in capturing domain-relevant information.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information in their representations.
Randomly initialized models can also encode useful features, sometimes on par with pretrained models.
Skip connections help preserve information across layers.
Pairwise probing can isolate the effect of specific properties and show causal relationships.
papers.abstract: Today we have a good theoretical understanding of the representational power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). For example, their limitations have been characterized in relation to a hierarchy of Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) isomorphism tests. However, we do not know what is encoded in the learned representations. This is our main question. We answer it using a probing framework to quantify the amount of meaningful information captured in graph representations. Our findings on molecular datasets show the potential of probing for understanding the inductive biases of graph-based models. We compare different families of models and show that transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information compared to models based on message passing. We also study the effect of different design choices such as skip connections and virtual nodes. We advocate for probing as a useful diagnostic tool for evaluating graph-based models.

papers.title: Counterfactual reasoning: an analysis of in-context emergence
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning, i.e., predicting consequences of hypothetical scenarios by inferring unobserved latent concepts and copying contextual noise from factual observations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models are capable of in-context counterfactual reasoning, and through analysis of Transformers, finds that self-attention, model depth, and pre-training data diversity drive performance, with mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and that designated noise abduction heads emerge.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can perform counterfactual reasoning by leveraging self-attention and depth, and this ability extends to sequential data, suggesting potential for counterfactual story generation.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning on synthetic linear regression tasks.
Self-attention is crucial for counterfactual reasoning; MLP-only models fail.
Model depth improves counterfactual reasoning performance.
Pre-training data diversity improves performance and out-of-distribution generalization.
The latent parameter is linearly encoded in the residual stream, and designated noise abduction heads emerge in attention layers.
papers.limitation: The synthetic setup may not fully capture the complexity of natural language counterfactual reasoning.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to natural language tasks and more complex functions.
Further exploration of the role of attention heads in counterfactual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit remarkable performance in in-context learning: the ability to learn and reason about the input context on the fly. This work studies in-context counterfactual reasoning in language models, that is, the ability to predict consequences of a hypothetical scenario. We focus on a well-defined, synthetic linear regression task that requires noise abduction. Accurate prediction is based on (1) inferring an unobserved latent concept and (2) copying contextual noise from factual observations. We show that language models are capable of counterfactual reasoning. Further, we enhance existing identifiability results and reduce counterfactual reasoning for a broad class of functions to a transformation on in-context observations. In Transformers, we find that self-attention, model depth and pre-training data diversity drive performance. Moreover, we provide mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and we introduce designated \textit{noise abduction heads} central to performing counterfactual reasoning. Lastly, our findings extend to counterfactual reasoning under SDE dynamics and reflect that Transformers can perform noise abduction on sequential data, providing preliminary evidence on the potential for counterfactual story generation. Our code is available under https://github.com/mrtzmllr/iccr.

papers.title: Explainable Molecular Property Prediction: Aligning Chemical Concepts with Predictions via Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we provide chemically meaningful and faithful explanations for molecular property predictions using language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Lamole, a framework for explainable molecular property prediction that uses Group SELFIES representation and combines attention weights with gradients, calibrated by a marginal loss, to provide chemically meaningful and faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: Lamole provides chemically meaningful and faithful explanations for molecular property prediction and can be integrated into an interpretable optimization pipeline for molecular design.
papers.key_findings:
Lamole achieves prediction accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art baselines while improving explanation accuracy by up to 14.3%.
The proposed information flow-based explanation method, integrating attention and gradients, captures interactions between functional groups.
The marginal loss aligns explanations with the tangent space of the data manifold, ensuring concept-aligned results.
Using only 10% of molecules with ground truth annotations can significantly improve explanation accuracy.
Integration with an evolutionary algorithm demonstrates Lamole's actionable utility for guiding molecular editing and optimization.
papers.limitation:
Complex interactions caused by multiple functional groups may not be fully captured, and other functional groups may receive relatively high importance scores.
The molecular editing case is a computational demonstration and does not imply real-world chemical optimality.
future_direction: Extending the framework to broader generalization scenarios, including unseen chemotypes.
Designing more strategies to reveal complex functional group interactions.
papers.abstract: Providing explainable molecular property predictions is critical for many scientific domains, such as drug discovery and material science. Though transformer-based language models have shown great potential in accurate molecular property prediction, they neither provide chemically meaningful explanations nor faithfully reveal the molecular structure-property relationships. In this work, we develop a framework for explainable molecular property prediction based on language models, dubbed as Lamole, which can provide chemical concepts-aligned explanations. We take a string-based molecular representation -- Group SELFIES -- as input tokens to pretrain and fine-tune our Lamole, as it provides chemically meaningful semantics. By disentangling the information flows of Lamole, we propose combining self-attention weights and gradients for better quantification of each chemically meaningful substructure's impact on the model's output. To make the explanations more faithfully respect the structure-property relationship, we then carefully craft a marginal loss to explicitly optimize the explanations to be able to align with the chemists' annotations. We bridge the manifold hypothesis with the elaborated marginal loss to prove that the loss can align the explanations with the tangent space of the data manifold, leading to concept-aligned explanations. Experimental results over six mutagenicity datasets and one hepatotoxicity dataset demonstrate Lamole can achieve comparable classification accuracy and boost the explanation accuracy by up to 14.3%, being the state-of-the-art in explainable molecular property prediction.

papers.title: Unveiling Latent Knowledge in Chemistry Language Models through Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do chemistry language models internally represent chemical knowledge, and can sparse autoencoders uncover interpretable features within these models?
papers.core_contribution: This work presents the first application of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to chemistry language models, revealing that these models encode a rich hierarchy of interpretable chemical features spanning structural motifs, physicochemical properties, and functional concepts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders can decompose the latent representations of a chemistry language model into an interpretable feature basis, revealing a rich landscape of chemically meaningful concepts and enabling causal manipulation of molecular structures.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features outperform individual neurons in detecting chemical substructures, especially rare ones, indicating a more disentangled representation.
SAE features provide a compact and decorrelated basis for aligning internal representations with external physicochemical descriptors.
Individual SAE features can capture higher-level functional concepts, such as grouping molecules by shared pharmacological activity (e.g., opioid receptor binding).
Feature steering via ablation demonstrates a causal link between specific features and the generation of corresponding chemical substructures or properties.
The SAE decomposition is information-preserving for downstream tasks (e.g., toxicity prediction) while isolating relevant signals into a more compact set of features than the original neuron basis.
papers.limitation:
The interpretation of features remains a presently unscaled process.
The analysis is confined to a single model architecture (SMI-TED).
The features discovered are contingent on the training data's chemical space, and their generalisation to out-of-distribution molecules remains an open question.
While features are compared to the raw neuron basis, more robust baselines are needed to fully validate the decomposition's effectiveness.
future_direction: Developing methods for the automated interpretation of chemical features.
Exploring applications in AI safety, such as identifying and ablating features correlated with undesirable properties (e.g., toxicity).
Investigating how features behave across different model architectures and scales, including exploring concepts like feature splitting.
papers.abstract: Since the advent of machine learning, interpretability has remained a persistent challenge, becoming increasingly urgent as generative models support high-stakes applications in drug and material discovery. Recent advances in large language model (LLM) architectures have yielded chemistry language models (CLMs) with impressive capabilities in molecular property prediction and molecular generation. However, how these models internally represent chemical knowledge remains poorly understood. In this work, we extend sparse autoencoder techniques to uncover and examine interpretable features within CLMs. Applying our methodology to the Foundation Models for Materials (FM4M) SMI-TED chemistry foundation model, we extract semantically meaningful latent features and analyse their activation patterns across diverse molecular datasets. Our findings reveal that these models encode a rich landscape of chemical concepts. We identify correlations between specific latent features and distinct domains of chemical knowledge, including structural motifs, physicochemical properties, and pharmacological drug classes. Our approach provides a generalisable framework for uncovering latent knowledge in chemistry-focused AI systems.
