papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for circuit identification using discrete sparse autoencoders trained on attention head outputs, which is more efficient and robust than existing techniques.
papers.conclusion: Discrete sparse autoencoders offer a scalable, efficient, and robust approach for circuit identification in large language models, providing a promising direction for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The method outperforms or matches state-of-the-art circuit identification techniques (ACDC, HISP, SP) in precision and recall on three tasks (IOI, Greater-than, Docstring).
The method is robust to hyperparameter choices and requires only 5-10 text examples per task to learn robust representations.
The identified circuits can match or even outperform the full model's performance on the specific tasks with fewer components.
The method can identify negative components in circuits (e.g., negative name-mover heads in IOI) that other algorithms struggle to find.
The process is significantly faster, reducing runtime from hours to seconds compared to existing methods.
papers.limitation: The method currently only analyzes attention heads and not other components like MLP layers, which may be important for some circuits (e.g., Greater-than).
future_direction: Extending the method to analyze MLP layers and other model components.
Applying the method to larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the use of vector-quantized variational autoencoders (VQ-VAEs) as an alternative to sparse autoencoders.
papers.abstract: This paper introduces an efficient and robust method for discovering interpretable circuits in large language models using discrete sparse autoencoders. Our approach addresses key limitations of existing techniques, namely computational complexity and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We propose training sparse autoencoders on carefully designed positive and negative examples, where the model can only correctly predict the next token for the positive examples. We hypothesise that learned representations of attention head outputs will signal when a head is engaged in specific computations. By discretising the learned representations into integer codes and measuring the overlap between codes unique to positive examples for each head, we enable direct identification of attention heads involved in circuits without the need for expensive ablations or architectural modifications. On three well-studied tasks - indirect object identification, greater-than comparisons, and docstring completion - the proposed method achieves higher precision and recall in recovering ground-truth circuits compared to state-of-the-art baselines, while reducing runtime from hours to seconds. Notably, we require only 5-10 text examples for each task to learn robust representations. Our findings highlight the promise of discrete sparse autoencoders for scalable and efficient mechanistic interpretability, offering a new direction for analysing the inner workings of large language models.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: Do neural nets learn statistical laws behind natural language?
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether neural language models can reproduce statistical laws of natural language, such as Zipf's law and Heaps' law, and examines their limitations in reproducing long-range correlation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that neural language models can reproduce Zipf's law and Heaps' law, statistical properties of natural language, but have a limitation in reproducing long-range correlation.
papers.conclusion: Neural language models can reproduce local statistical patterns (Zipf's and Heaps' laws) but not global long-range correlation, indicating a limitation in capturing the global structure of natural language.
papers.key_findings:
Neural language models (stacked LSTM) can reproduce Zipf's law for n-grams, including long n-grams.
Neural language models reproduce Heaps' law, though with a slightly larger exponent than the original text.
The models learn these statistical laws gradually during training, starting from a monkey-typing-like state.
The models fail to reproduce long-range correlation as measured by the autocorrelation function for intervals between rare words.
The generated pseudo-text has predictability situated between word-shuffled and document-shuffled versions of the original text.
papers.limitation:
The neural language model cannot reproduce long-range correlation in natural language.
The exponent for Heaps' law in generated text is larger than in the original text.
future_direction: Exploring conditions to reproduce the long-range correlation in text with language models, including both stochastic and neural language models.
Testing new neural models with enhanced long-memory features, such as CNNs or hierarchical RNNs.
papers.abstract: The performance of deep learning in natural language processing has been spectacular, but the reasons for this success remain unclear because of the inherent complexity of deep learning. This paper provides empirical evidence of its effectiveness and of a limitation of neural networks for language engineering. Precisely, we demonstrate that a neural language model based on long short-term memory (LSTM) effectively reproduces Zipf's law and Heaps' law, two representative statistical properties underlying natural language. We discuss the quality of reproducibility and the emergence of Zipf's law and Heaps' law as training progresses. We also point out that the neural language model has a limitation in reproducing long-range correlation, another statistical property of natural language. This understanding could provide a direction for improving the architectures of neural networks.

papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: What are the primary mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in large language models during continual fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three primary mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during sequential fine-tuning: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening around prior task minima.
papers.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in LLMs is driven by three interacting mechanisms (attention disruption, representational drift, loss landscape flattening), providing a mechanistic foundation for developing targeted continual learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 15-23% of attention heads, particularly in lower layers, undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, driving early forgetting.
Representational drift in intermediate layers, measured by CKA similarity, decreases by 0.32 to 0.47, indicating significant geometric changes.
Gradient interference, especially in query and key projection matrices, strongly predicts forgetting severity (correlation r=0.87).
The loss landscape around previous task minima flattens substantially (maximum Hessian eigenvalue drops from 147.3 to 34.2), making recovery difficult.
These three mechanisms interact and operate at different timescales, with attention disruption early, representational drift accumulating, and landscape flattening emerging later.
papers.limitation:
Experimental design focused on task sequences with clear boundaries, not continuous adaptation to gradually shifting distributions.
Examined forgetting over relatively short task sequences (4 to 6 tasks), while practical systems may encounter hundreds of sequential tasks.
Mechanistic analysis primarily characterized average behaviors across many model instances; understanding individual variability and rare failure modes remains important.
future_direction: Developing architecture modifications that inherently resist the identified forgetting mechanisms, such as attention heads with built-in stability constraints or intermediate layers with protected representational subspaces.
Designing optimization algorithms that explicitly manage gradient interference, representational drift, and landscape geometry during fine-tuning.
Creating diagnostic tools that monitor mechanistic signatures in real-time to prevent catastrophic forgetting before it occurs.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit remarkable performance across diverse tasks through pre-training and fine-tuning paradigms. However, continual fine-tuning on sequential tasks induces catastrophic forgetting, where newly acquired knowledge interferes with previously learned capabilities. Despite widespread observations of this phenomenon, the mechanistic understanding remains limited. Here, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of catastrophic forgetting in transformer-based LLMs during sequential fine-tuning. Through systematic experiments across multiple model scales (109B to 400B total parameters) and task sequences, we identify three primary mechanisms driving forgetting: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening. We demonstrate that forgetting severity correlates strongly with task similarity (Pearson r = 0.87) and gradient alignment metrics. Our analysis reveals that approximately 15 to 23 percent of attention heads undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, with lower layers showing greater susceptibility. These findings establish mechanistic foundations for developing targeted mitigation strategies in continual learning systems.

papers.title: How much do contextualized representations encode long-range context?
papers.research_question: How much do contextualized representations encode long-range context?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents an analysis of how much contextualized representations in autoregressive language models encode long-range context, using a perturbation setup and a new metric (ACCS). It finds that similar perplexity can mask differences in downstream performance, which is explained by varying degrees of long-range contextualization.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides representation-level insights into long-range context encoding, showing the benefits of hybrid architectures and larger model sizes, and suggests directions for improving long-context language models.
papers.key_findings:
Models with similar perplexity can achieve markedly different downstream task performance, which correlates with the degree to which their hidden representations are contextualized by long-range content (measured by ACCS).
Models exhibit increasingly anisotropic representations as the input prefix becomes less compressible (i.e., has a higher compression rate).
Fully recurrent models (e.g., Mamba-2, mLSTM) and Transformers with ALiBi positional encoding rely primarily on local context for prediction.
RoPE-based Transformers can over-contextualize distant context, including noise, when tested on sequences longer than their pre-training length.
Hybrid models (e.g., Griffin, HybridMamba) more effectively contextualize the entire sequence structure, balancing local and global context without over-relying on either.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is conducted over ten language models and could be extended to more recent architectures and open-access models.
The perturbation operation is constrained to simple token shuffling; other perturbations (e.g., maintaining n-gram statistics) could provide further insights.
Experiments on synthetic sequences were limited to the simplest possible regularity (periodic repetition).
The analysis primarily focused on base models with limited investigation on aligned models and no exploration on practical scenarios like reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Examining other more recent architectures and open-access models.
Investigating other perturbation operations beyond token shuffling.
Exploring other regularities in synthetic sequences to inspect model generalization.
papers.abstract: We analyze contextual representations in neural autoregressive language models, emphasizing long-range contexts that span several thousand tokens. Our methodology employs a perturbation setup and the metric \emph{Anisotropy-Calibrated Cosine Similarity}, to capture the degree of contextualization of long-range patterns from the perspective of representation geometry. We begin the analysis with a case study on standard decoder-only Transformers, demonstrating that similar perplexity can exhibit markedly different downstream task performance, which can be explained by the difference in contextualization of long-range content. Next, we extend the analysis to other models, covering recent novel architectural designs and various training configurations. The representation-level results illustrate a reduced capacity for high-complexity (i.e., less compressible) sequences across architectures, and that fully recurrent models rely heavily on local context, whereas hybrid models more effectively encode the entire sequence structure. Finally, preliminary analysis of model size and training configurations on the encoding of long-range context suggest potential directions for improving existing language models.

papers.title: Why Can't Transformers Learn Multiplication? Reverse-Engineering Reveals Long-Range Dependency Pitfalls
papers.research_question: Why do transformers fail to learn multi-digit multiplication?
papers.core_contribution: By reverse-engineering a successful implicit chain-of-thought model, the paper uncovers that transformers fail at multiplication due to a lack of long-range dependencies, and demonstrates that an auxiliary loss providing the correct inductive bias can enable learning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers fail to learn multi-digit multiplication due to a pitfall in learning long-range dependencies with gradient descent and an auto-regressive loss, but this can be addressed with the correct inductive bias, as demonstrated by the auxiliary loss method.
papers.key_findings:
The ICoT model learns the necessary long-range dependencies for multi-digit multiplication, while standard fine-tuning does not.
The ICoT model encodes long-range dependencies via attention patterns that form a directed acyclic graph (attention tree) to cache and retrieve pairwise partial products.
The ICoT model implements partial products in attention heads as Minkowski sums and represents digits using a Fourier basis, forming an efficient pentagonal prism structure.
Standard fine-tuning converges to a local optimum that lacks the required long-range dependencies, causing loss to plateau on middle digits.
An auxiliary loss that supervises the prediction of a 'running partial sum' via a linear regression probe provides an inductive bias that enables the model to learn multiplication successfully.
papers.limitation: The suggested inductive bias is task-specific and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Developing generalizing inductive biases for tasks with long-range dependencies.
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly capable, yet still fail at a seemingly simple task of multi-digit multiplication. In this work, we study why, by reverse-engineering a model that successfully learns multiplication via \emph{implicit chain-of-thought}, and report three findings: (1) Evidence of long-range structure: Logit attributions and linear probes indicate that the model encodes the necessary long-range dependencies for multi-digit multiplication. (2) Mechanism: the model encodes long-range dependencies using attention to construct a directed acyclic graph to ``cache'' and ``retrieve'' pairwise partial products. (3) Geometry: the model implements partial products in attention heads by forming Minkowski sums between pairs of digits, and digits are represented using a Fourier basis, both of which are intuitive and efficient representations that the standard fine-tuning model lacks. With these insights, we revisit the learning dynamics of standard fine-tuning and find that the model converges to a local optimum that lacks the required long-range dependencies. We further validate this understanding by introducing an auxiliary loss that predicts the ``running sum'' via a linear regression probe, which provides an inductive bias that enables the model to successfully learn multi-digit multiplication. In summary, by reverse-engineering the mechanisms of an implicit chain-of-thought model we uncover a pitfall for learning long-range dependencies in Transformers and provide an example of how the correct inductive bias can address this issue.

papers.title: A Polar coordinate system represents syntax in large language models
papers.research_question: How are syntactic relations (type and direction) represented in the activations of large language models? Specifically, are they coded by a polar coordinate system where distance and relative direction between word embeddings represent the existence and type of syntactic relations?
papers.core_contribution: This work shows that syntactic trees are represented in LLMs by a polar coordinate system where distance and direction between word embeddings encode the existence and type of syntactic relations, and introduces the Polar Probe, a linear readout method that recovers this structure.
papers.conclusion: LLMs spontaneously learn a geometry of neural activations that explicitly represents the main symbolic structures of linguistic theory, reconciling symbolic and connectionist formalisms.
papers.key_findings:
The Polar Probe successfully recovers the type and direction of syntactic relations, substantially outperforming the Structural Probe by nearly two folds.
The polar coordinate system exists in a low-dimensional subspace of the intermediate layers of many LLMs and becomes increasingly precise in the latest frontier models.
Similar syntactic relations are coded similarly across the nested levels of syntactic trees, as demonstrated on a controlled dataset.
papers.limitation:
Only the English language is investigated, limiting generalization to other languages with different grammatical rules.
Syntactic structures are not necessarily restricted to words; morphology predicts that words themselves may be represented as trees of morphemes, which is not explored.
The Polar Probe is based on a supervised task requiring known syntactic structures; an unsupervised probe would be important for discovering unsuspected structures.
The work assumes Euclidean probes; alternative assumptions like hyperbolic representations could be fruitful but are not explored.
future_direction: Exploring universal (or divergent) grammatical representations in artificial neural networks across languages.
Investigating whether the framework generalizes to different scales of linguistic structures, such as morphology.
Developing an unsupervised probe to discover unsuspected syntactic structures.
Testing alternative linguistic theories (e.g., phrase structures) with the probing framework.
Exploring hyperbolic or other non-Euclidean representations for syntactic trees.
papers.abstract: Originally formalized with symbolic representations, syntactic trees may also be effectively represented in the activations of large language models (LLMs). Indeed, a 'Structural Probe' can find a subspace of neural activations, where syntactically related words are relatively close to one-another. However, this syntactic code remains incomplete: the distance between the Structural Probe word embeddings can represent the existence but not the type and direction of syntactic relations. Here, we hypothesize that syntactic relations are, in fact, coded by the relative direction between nearby embeddings. To test this hypothesis, we introduce a 'Polar Probe' trained to read syntactic relations from both the distance and the direction between word embeddings. Our approach reveals three main findings. First, our Polar Probe successfully recovers the type and direction of syntactic relations, and substantially outperforms the Structural Probe by nearly two folds. Second, we confirm that this polar coordinate system exists in a low-dimensional subspace of the intermediate layers of many LLMs and becomes increasingly precise in the latest frontier models. Third, we demonstrate with a new benchmark that similar syntactic relations are coded similarly across the nested levels of syntactic trees. Overall, this work shows that LLMs spontaneously learn a geometry of neural activations that explicitly represents the main symbolic structures of linguistic theory.

papers.title: Stream: Scaling up Mechanistic Interpretability to Long Context in LLMs via Sparse Attention
papers.research_question: How to scale mechanistic interpretability techniques to long contexts in LLMs, given the quadratic scaling of attention? Specifically, how to efficiently analyze attention patterns in long contexts with near-linear time and memory?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SPARSETRACING and STREAM, a scalable framework and algorithm for mechanistic interpretability in long-context LLMs, achieving near-linear time and linear memory complexity by leveraging hierarchical sparse attention pruning.
papers.conclusion: SPARSETRACING and STREAM provide scalable tools for mechanistic interpretability in long-context LLMs, enabling experiments previously infeasible due to quadratic complexity, and democratizing long-context interpretability on consumer hardware.
papers.key_findings:
STREAM prunes 97-99% of attention links in chain-of-thought reasoning traces while preserving model output, identifying thought anchors.
On the RULER benchmark, STREAM preserves critical retrieval paths while discarding 90-96% of interactions, exposing layer-wise routes from needle to output.
STREAM enables interpretability of million-token contexts on consumer GPUs, reducing resource costs by up to four orders of magnitude.
Needle retrieval is more robust for needles earlier in the context, and pruning weakens retrieval towards the end of longer contexts.
STREAM's sparse masks highlight the same key structures as dense patterns but with linear scaling, making long-context interpretability feasible.
papers.limitation:
STREAM focuses only on the attention mechanism and does not account for residual connections and MLP layers.
The method's success is defined by a proxy metric (two consecutive correct tokens), which may not fully capture model performance or complete causal paths.
The current implementation is not optimized for specific hardware and runs slower than desired.
The pruning algorithm is more aggressive towards the bottom of the attention pattern, which could be resolved by implementing variable sparsity constant k.
Future work introducing a novel discovery made by STREAM would truly validate the method's applicability.
future_direction: Incorporate MLP layers and residual stream analysis into the SPARSETRACING framework.
Establish theoretical guarantees about what types of circuits and information pathways are preserved under different sparsity levels.
Use STREAM to study long context phenomena like information over-squashing, over-smoothing, and under-reaching.
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) scale to million-token contexts, traditional Mechanistic Interpretability techniques for analyzing attention scale quadratically with context length, demanding terabytes of memory beyond 100,000 tokens. We introduce Sparse Tracing, a novel technique that leverages dynamic sparse attention to efficiently analyze long context attention patterns. We present Stream, a compilable hierarchical pruning algorithm that estimates per-head sparse attention masks in near-linear time $O(T \log T)$ and linear space $O(T)$, enabling one-pass interpretability at scale. Stream performs a binary-search-style refinement to retain only the top-$k$ key blocks per query while preserving the model's next-token behavior. We apply Stream to long chain-of-thought reasoning traces and identify thought anchors while pruning 97-99\% of token interactions. On the RULER benchmark, Stream preserves critical retrieval paths while discarding 90-96\% of interactions and exposes layer-wise routes from the needle to output. Our method offers a practical drop-in tool for analyzing attention patterns and tracing information flow without terabytes of caches. By making long context interpretability feasible on consumer GPUs, Sparse Tracing helps democratize chain-of-thought monitoring. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/stream-03B8/.

papers.title: Attention Mechanisms Perspective: Exploring LLM Processing of Graph-Structured Data
papers.research_question: How do LLMs process graph-structured data from the perspective of attention mechanisms, and do they effectively utilize graph connectivity information?
papers.core_contribution: This paper empirically studies LLM attention on graph-structured data, finding that LLMs struggle to model inter-node relationships due to architectural constraints, and that intermediate attention windows (neither fully connected nor fixed-link) improve training and inference performance.
papers.conclusion: The work explores LLM attention mechanisms on graph data, discovers multiple phenomena, and provides directional guidance for future research in graph machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can recognize graph data and capture text-node interactions but struggle to model inter-node relationships within graph structures.
The attention distribution of LLMs across graph nodes does not align with ideal structural patterns, indicating a failure to adapt to graph topology nuances.
Neither fully connected attention nor fixed connectivity is optimal; intermediate-state attention windows improve LLM training performance and transfer well to fully connected windows during inference.
The study identifies 'Attention Sink' issues similar to NLP tasks and a unique 'Skewed Line Sink' phenomenon specific to graph data.
Training LLMs with a smaller linkage horizon (incorporating some topological information) and then transferring to a larger horizon during inference enhances performance and addresses deployment challenges.
papers.limitation: Due to limitations in length and resources, only a portion of the discovered phenomena were analyzed; many unexplored phenomena remain.
future_direction: Explore methods to correct attention biases (e.g., Attention Sink and Skewed Line Sink) to improve model performance.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms are critical to the success of large language models (LLMs), driving significant advancements in multiple fields. However, for graph-structured data, which requires emphasis on topological connections, they fall short compared to message-passing mechanisms on fixed links, such as those employed by Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). This raises a question: ``Does attention fail for graphs in natural language settings?'' Motivated by these observations, we embarked on an empirical study from the perspective of attention mechanisms to explore how LLMs process graph-structured data. The goal is to gain deeper insights into the attention behavior of LLMs over graph structures. We uncovered unique phenomena regarding how LLMs apply attention to graph-structured data and analyzed these findings to improve the modeling of such data by LLMs. The primary findings of our research are: 1) While LLMs can recognize graph data and capture text-node interactions, they struggle to model inter-node relationships within graph structures due to inherent architectural constraints. 2) The attention distribution of LLMs across graph nodes does not align with ideal structural patterns, indicating a failure to adapt to graph topology nuances. 3) Neither fully connected attention nor fixed connectivity is optimal; each has specific limitations in its application scenarios. Instead, intermediate-state attention windows improve LLM training performance and seamlessly transition to fully connected windows during inference. Source code: \href{https://github.com/millioniron/LLM_exploration}{LLM4Exploration}

papers.title: “Amide − amine + alcohol = carboxylic acid.” chemical reactions as linear algebraic analogies in graph neural networks
papers.research_question: Do graph neural network (GNN) atom-embeddings exhibit linear algebraic analogies similar to word embeddings in NLP, and how do these analogies relate to chemical reactions and properties?
papers.core_contribution: Atom-embeddings in pretrained graph neural networks exhibit linear algebraic analogies that correspond to chemical reactions, revealing a highly structured latent space that mirrors chemical syntax.
papers.conclusion: The latent space of GNNs in chemistry is highly structured and organized according to chemical syntax, with linear analogies providing a global explanatory framework for chemical transformations and properties.
papers.key_findings:
Atom-embeddings in a pretrained GNN (SchNet) show arithmetic properties allowing linear analogies that represent valid chemical reaction formulas, similar to word analogies in NLP.
Reaction vectors (differences between reactant and product embeddings) are approximately constant for a given reaction type and are colinear for similar reactions (e.g., oxidations).
The linear analogies can be explained by a perturbational replicate model based on neighborhood chemical composition, linking the embedding structure to chemical principles.
The structured embedding space facilitates transfer learning and reveals linear relations in chemical properties like NMR chemical shifts and atomization energies.
The organization of the embedding space has two levels: substructure composition and changes to substructure, with similar changes aligning in direction.
papers.limitation:
The QM9 dataset only includes equilibrium geometries, so the reaction datasets only account for initial and product states, not mechanistic transitions.
Geometry optimization using force fields may introduce non-equilibrium geometries from the perspective of the DFT-trained model.
The replicate model is an approximation and ignores the exact layout of the graph.
future_direction: Mapping out the trajectories of reactions in the latent space to study transition states.
Studying how the global explanatory framework reduces to local explanations on a case-by-case basis.
Improving the replicate model by incorporating the exact graph layout and using the same geometry optimization as the GNN model.
papers.abstract: In deep learning methods, especially in the context of chemistry, there is an increasing urgency to uncover the hidden learning mechanisms often dubbed as "black box." In this work, we show that graph models built on computational chemical data behave similar to natural language processing (NLP) models built on text data. Crucially, we show that atom-embeddings, a.k.a atom-parsed graph neural activation patterns, exhibit arithmetic properties that represent valid reaction formulas. This is very similar to how word-embeddings can be combined to make word analogies, thus preserving the semantic meaning behind the words, as in the famous example "King" - "Man" + "Woman" = "Queen." For instance, we show how the reaction from an alcohol to a carbonyl is represented by a constant vector in the embedding space, implicitly representing "-H<sub>2</sub>." This vector is independent from the particular carbonyl reactant and alcohol product and represents a consistent chemical transformation. Other directions in the embedding space are synonymous with distinct chemical changes (ex. the tautomerization direction). In contrast to natural language processing, we can explain the observed chemical analogies using algebraic manipulations on the local chemical composition that surrounds each atom-embedding. Furthermore, the observations find applications in transfer learning, for instance in the formal structure and prediction of atomistic properties, such as <sup>1</sup>H-NMR and <sup>13</sup>C-NMR. This work is in line with the recent push for interpretable explanations to graph neural network modeling of chemistry and uncovers a latent model of chemistry that is highly structured, consistent, and analogous to chemical syntax.

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of\n Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the stacked layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interventional, input perturbation-based analysis method to show that Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, with larger contexts and more complex phrase boundaries becoming more salient in deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process; structured input perturbations are a useful tool for analyzing deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing characteristic scale of context along layers.
Swapping two constituent phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrase spans of the same length, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, indicating sensitivity to phrase hierarchy.
Changes in attention weights partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance, with deeper layers showing more correlation.
The observed sensitivities are not due to simple co-occurrence statistics, as shown by controlling for PMI.
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features
Searching for the causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance
Exploring applications in network pruning studies
Extending the method as a hypothesis generator in neuroscience to understand compositional structure in neural populations
papers.abstract:
While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models
have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete
accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear
what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations,
nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In
this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of
interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from
pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive
neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of
probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several
kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a
sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the
original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random
permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a
representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which
do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase
structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break
apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure.
 Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build
sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that
hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our
results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of
analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can
serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for
interpreting complex black-box models.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Deconstructing Attention: Investigating Design Principles for Effective Language Modeling
papers.research_question: Which design principles of dot-product attention are essential for effective language modeling, and can some be relaxed in hybrid architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Token mixing is indispensable for language modeling, while the mathematical form and sequence dependency can be relaxed, especially in hybrid architectures where standard attention layers stabilize simpler variants.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that token mixing is essential, but other attention principles can be simplified, especially when standard attention layers are interleaved, leading to robust performance.
papers.key_findings:
Token mixing is crucial; without it, models perform near-random on NLU tasks.
The standard mathematical form is important in uniform configurations but can be relaxed in hybrid ones.
Sequence-dependency enhances generalization ability.
Current QK derivation is not as essential as expected.
Layer collaboration allows poor-performing variants to contribute in hybrid architectures.
papers.limitation: Experiments are limited to models up to 500M parameters, 15B tokens pretraining, and monolingual tokenizer.
future_direction: Experimenting with larger models and different model families.
papers.abstract: The success of Transformer language models is widely credited to their dot-product attention mechanism, which interweaves a set of key design principles: mixing information across positions (enabling multi-token interactions), sequence-dependent activations (where attention weights adapt to each input), a specific mathematical form (dot-product similarities plus softmax weighting), and coupling of queries and keys to evolving hidden states (grounding attention in the current layer). However, the necessity of each of these principles remains largely untested. In this work, we systematically deconstruct attention by designing controlled variants that selectively relax these principles, applied both uniformly across all layers and in hybrid architectures where only some layers retain standard attention. Our empirical analysis reveals that mechanisms for mixing tokens are indispensable, as their absence collapses models to near-random behavior, while the exact mathematical form and sequence dependency can be substantially relaxed, especially when preserved in just a subset of layers. Surprisingly, even variants that fail in isolation can achieve robust performance when interleaved with standard attention, highlighting a cooperative effect. These findings deepen our understanding of what truly underpins attention's effectiveness and open new avenues for simplifying language models without sacrificing performance.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task
papers.research_question: Does a sequence model trained on a synthetic task (Othello game transcripts) learn an internal representation of the board state, and is that representation causal to its predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that a GPT model trained on Othello game transcripts learns a nonlinear internal representation of the board state, which is causally involved in its predictions. It introduces intervention techniques and latent saliency maps for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide evidence that Othello-GPT maintains a nonlinear internal representation of the game board state, which is causally linked to its predictions. The tools introduced (nonlinear probes, interventions, latent saliency maps) may prove useful for interpretability in natural language settings.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT predicts legal moves with high accuracy, and this is not due to memorization.
Nonlinear probes can accurately decode the board state from internal activations, while linear probes perform poorly.
Intervention experiments show that the board representation is causal to the model's predictions.
Latent saliency maps reveal differences between models trained on synthetic vs. championship data, indicating different learned strategies.
The internal representation of the board state is nonlinear and emerges during training.
papers.limitation: Latent saliency maps only attribute to one tile when multiple tiles are involved in a move, which does not fully capture the Othello rule logic.
future_direction: Extend investigation to other, more complex games.
Compare strategies learned by a sequence model with those of a model trained with a priori knowledge of Othello.
Study how results generalize to natural language models.
papers.abstract: Language models show a surprising range of capabilities, but the source of their apparent competence is unclear. Do these networks just memorize a collection of surface statistics, or do they rely on internal representations of the process that generates the sequences they see? We investigate this question by applying a variant of the GPT model to the task of predicting legal moves in a simple board game, Othello. Although the network has no a priori knowledge of the game or its rules, we uncover evidence of an emergent nonlinear internal representation of the board state. Interventional experiments indicate this representation can be used to control the output of the network and create "latent saliency maps" that can help explain predictions in human terms.

papers.title: MindCraft: How Concept Trees Take Shape In Deep Models
papers.research_question: How do neural networks internally construct and consolidate abstract concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the MindCraft framework and Concept Trees to systematically trace how abstract concepts emerge, branch, and stabilize across layers in deep models.
papers.conclusion: MindCraft provides a hierarchical reconstruction of a model's reasoning process, offering a significant step towards building transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Trees reveal a hierarchical, tree-shaped organization of concept separation within models, with more salient concepts branching earlier.
The method captures conceptual importance shaped by context, not just token embedding distances.
Propagation patterns of counterfactual differences are consistent across diverse tasks, indicating a robust hierarchical dynamic.
Concept separation layers are disentangled from input embedding distances, highlighting the framework's ability to analyze high-level conceptual organization.
The framework is applicable across multiple model architectures and scales, demonstrating generality.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-modal domains.
Using the identified Concept Paths to perform precise, surgical edits on model behavior.
Exploring the compositional 'algebra' of how multiple concepts interact within the network's learned representation space.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models demonstrate strong performance across language, vision, and reasoning tasks. However, how they internally structure and stabilize concepts remains elusive. Inspired by causal inference, we introduce the MindCraft framework built upon Concept Trees. By applying spectral decomposition at each layer and linking principal directions into branching Concept Paths, Concept Trees reconstruct the hierarchical emergence of concepts, revealing exactly when they diverge from shared representations into linearly separable subspaces. Empirical evaluations across diverse scenarios across disciplines, including medical diagnosis, physics reasoning, and political decision-making, show that Concept Trees recover semantic hierarchies, disentangle latent concepts, and can be widely applied across multiple domains. The Concept Tree establishes a widely applicable and powerful framework that enables in-depth analysis of conceptual representations in deep models, marking a significant step forward in the foundation of interpretable AI.

papers.title: Garbage Attention in Large Language Models: BOS Sink Heads and Sink-aware Pruning
papers.research_question: What explains the layer-wise sensitivity and redundancy in LLMs, particularly in higher layers, and how can the <BOS> sink phenomenon be leveraged for effective pruning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies <BOS> sink heads as a key mechanism for redundancy in LLMs and proposes a sink-aware pruning strategy that effectively removes redundant components with minimal performance loss.
papers.conclusion: The <BOS> sink phenomenon is a primary driver of functional redundancy in LLMs, and sink-aware pruning based on <BOS> sink scores provides an efficient and effective method for model compression, matching or exceeding established pruning methods.
papers.key_findings:
Heads with high <BOS> sink scores are functionally redundant, showing negligible impact on performance when ablated.
High <BOS> sink heads are concentrated in deeper layers, explaining the layer-wise sensitivity observed in pruning studies.
Pruning based on <BOS> sink scores outperforms magnitude- and activation-based methods (e.g., Wanda-SP, Mag-SP) in preserving downstream task accuracy.
The behavior of sink heads is stable across varying input sequence lengths, with higher-scoring heads showing more gradual decline in attention scores as sequence length increases.
The <BOS> sink score serves as a robust structural metric for identifying redundant heads and layers, enabling effective structured pruning.
papers.limitation:
The work is empirical and does not provide a formal theoretical derivation for the positional concentration of sink heads in deeper layers.
The study is limited to models of specific scales (e.g., 4B and 8B parameters) and may not generalize to ultra-large scale models.
future_direction: Validate the <BOS> sink phenomenon across larger-scale models and a broader range of downstream tasks.
Investigate whether similar attention-anchoring mechanisms exist in other Transformer-based architectures beyond text, such as Vision-Language Models (VLMs).
Study the developmental dynamics of sink heads during the pre-training phase to understand how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to contain significant redundancy, yet a systematic explanation for why certain components, particularly in higher layers, are more redundant has remained elusive. In this work, we identify the BOS sink phenomenon as a key mechanism driving this layer-wise sensitivity. We show that attention heads with high BOS sink scores are strongly associated with functional redundancy: such heads, especially in deeper layers, contribute little to predictive performance and effectively serve as \emph{dumping grounds} for superfluous attention weights. This provides a concrete functional explanation for the structural redundancy reported in prior studies. Leveraging this insight, we introduce a simple pruning strategy that removes high-BOS sink heads. Experiments on Gemma-3, Llama-3.1, and Qwen3 demonstrate that this approach identifies redundant transformer components more reliably than weight- or activation-based criteria, while preserving performance close to dense baselines even under aggressive pruning. Moreover, we find that the behavior of sink heads remains stable across different sequence lengths. Overall, our results suggest that structural properties of attention offer a more intuitive and robust basis for model compression than magnitude-based methods.

papers.title: See What You Are Told: Visual Attention Sink in Large Multimodal Models
papers.research_question: What causes the visual attention sink phenomenon in large multimodal models, and how can attention be redistributed from sink tokens to improve model performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies the visual attention sink phenomenon in large multimodal models and proposes Visual Attention Redistribution (VAR), a training-free method that reallocates attention from sink tokens to non-sink visual tokens, improving model performance on various vision-language tasks.
papers.conclusion: The visual attention sink phenomenon exists in LMMs, and redistributing attention via VAR improves model performance by enhancing focus on images, offering a new perspective on understanding attention mechanisms in LMMs.
papers.key_findings:
LMMs exhibit visual attention sink, where irrelevant visual tokens receive high attention weights due to massive activation in specific hidden state dimensions.
Visual sink tokens do not contribute to model output and can be removed without performance loss.
The attention from sink tokens can be redistributed to non-sink visual tokens to enhance image focus.
VAR improves performance on general vision-language, visual hallucination, and vision-centric tasks across multiple LMMs.
VAR can be applied without additional training, models, or inference steps.
papers.limitation: Token masking experiments induce out-of-distribution behavior and have inconsistencies in random knockout across layers.
future_direction: Investigation of how visual tokens are recognized as sink tokens during training.
papers.abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) "see" images by leveraging the attention mechanism between text and visual tokens in the transformer decoder. Ideally, these models should focus on key visual information relevant to the text token. However, recent findings indicate that LMMs have an extraordinary tendency to consistently allocate high attention weights to specific visual tokens, even when these tokens are irrelevant to the corresponding text. In this study, we investigate the property behind the appearance of these irrelevant visual tokens and examine their characteristics. Our findings show that this behavior arises due to the massive activation of certain hidden state dimensions, which resembles the attention sink found in language models. Hence, we refer to this phenomenon as the visual attention sink. In particular, our analysis reveals that removing the irrelevant visual sink tokens does not impact model performance, despite receiving high attention weights. Consequently, we recycle the attention to these tokens as surplus resources, redistributing the attention budget to enhance focus on the image. To achieve this, we introduce Visual Attention Redistribution (VAR), a method that redistributes attention in image-centric heads, which we identify as innately focusing on visual information. VAR can be seamlessly applied across different LMMs to improve performance on a wide range of tasks, including general vision-language tasks, visual hallucination tasks, and vision-centric tasks, all without the need for additional training, models, or inference steps. Experimental results demonstrate that VAR enables LMMs to process visual information more effectively by adjusting their internal attention mechanisms, offering a new direction to enhancing the multimodal capabilities of LMMs.

papers.title: Understanding the patterns that neural networks learn from chemical spectra
papers.research_question: How does a neural network learn to classify infrared spectra of small organic molecules by functional groups, and what specific patterns (both intuitive and non-intuitive) does it use for classification?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a simpler 1D CNN that achieves state-of-the-art performance for functional group classification in infrared spectra and introduces a two-step explainability approach, revealing the network uses both characteristic group frequencies and non-intuitive patterns like tails and overtones.
papers.conclusion: The simplified CNN model is effective for spectral classification, and the explainability approach reveals the network uses both intuitive and non-intuitive spectral patterns, which can help assess generalization and guide future model design incorporating physics-based knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The 1D CNN achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art models while being significantly less complex.
The model consistently attends to the same spectral regions across different random initializations, indicating robust feature learning.
The network learns to use characteristic group frequencies (peaks) for classification, aligning with expert knowledge.
The network also uses non-intuitive patterns such as tails and anharmonic vibrations (overtones and combination bands) to improve classification certainty.
For some functional groups (e.g., nitriles), class imbalance and the presence of only one characteristic band lead to poor classification accuracy, highlighting dataset limitations.
papers.limitation:
Class imbalance leads to poor classification accuracy for rare functional groups like nitriles.
The network sometimes uses non-characteristic vibrations (e.g., C-H wags for halides) which may not generalize to new datasets.
future_direction: Incorporate physics-based intuition into model design, e.g., using IR tables to initialize parameters or filters that optimally recognize peaks.
Transfer understanding from pretrained models to new datasets (potentially from different spectral regions).
papers.abstract: We train a convolutional neural network to classify functional groups from infrared spectra. With explainability methods, we show the model uses the presence and absence of peaks, at fundamental and anharmonic frequencies for accurate classification.

papers.title: Where to Add PDE Diffusion in Transformers
papers.research_question: Where should a local PDE diffusion layer be inserted relative to attention in Transformers to improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an operator-theoretic framework for inserting a local PDE diffusion layer in Transformers, showing that early insertion (e.g., after embedding) acts as beneficial pre-regularization, while post-attention insertion is harmful due to non-commutativity between diffusion and attention.
papers.conclusion: Operator-theoretic reasoning can predict insertion-position sensitivity for local-global compositions in Transformers, with early diffusion providing beneficial pre-regularization and post-attention diffusion being structurally harmful.
papers.key_findings:
Inserting PDE diffusion after the embedding layer improves average accuracy by +4.1 percentage points on the Long Range Arena benchmark.
Inserting PDE diffusion after attention degrades performance by -2.5 percentage points, consistent with a predicted double-mixing conflict.
The effect of diffusion depends on the local roughness of representations at the insertion point and the downstream amplification of perturbations.
Diffusion and attention are non-commuting operators, leading to representational discrepancy when applied in different orders.
A multi-scale diffusion variant under the same global stability budget yields consistent gains by covering multiple frequency bands.
papers.limitation:
The claims are scoped to a spectrally-budgeted PDE diffusion operator and controlled long-sequence benchmarks (LRA) with moderate model sizes and contexts.
The study does not directly measure geometric diagnostics (e.g., commutator norms) and the multi-scale ablation is limited in task coverage.
future_direction: Mechanistic validation by measuring roughness and commutator statistics across depth.
Scaling to language modeling benchmarks and larger models.

Integrating PDE diffusion more tightly inside attention computations and applying the operator-theoretic lens to other hybrid local-global modules (e.g., convolution-attention, state-space-attention).
papers.abstract: Transformers enable powerful content-based global routing via self-attention, but they lack an explicit local geometric prior along the sequence axis. As a result, the placement of locality-inducing modules in hybrid architectures has largely been empirical. We study a simple deterministic PDE diffusion layer implemented as one explicit Euler step of one-dimensional heat smoothing using a discrete Neumann Laplacian under a spectral stability constraint, and ask a structural question: where should diffusion be inserted relative to attention? Our central claim is that diffusion and attention generally do not commute, so inserting the same local operator before versus after attention leads to qualitatively different behaviors. We develop a three-layer operator-theoretic framework that (1) establishes unconditional guarantees for the diffusion subsystem, including spectral non-expansiveness and monotone Dirichlet-energy dissipation when the diffusion step size is smaller than one half, (2) derives compositional perturbation bounds linking insertion effects to representation roughness and downstream amplification, and (3) uses diffusion-attention non-commutativity as a diagnostic for structural double-mixing conflicts. Guided by theory, we evaluate seven insertion positions on the Long Range Arena benchmark. Early diffusion acts as effective pre-regularization, improving average accuracy by 4.1 percentage points when applied after embedding, while post-attention diffusion degrades performance by 2.5 percentage points, consistent with the predicted conflict. A multi-scale diffusion variant yields consistent gains under the same global stability constraint. Our analysis provides a general template for reasoning about local-global compositions in sequence models by separating provable guarantees, compositional bounds, and mechanistic diagnostics.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Graph-Aware Isomorphic Attention for Adaptive Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can graph-aware relational reasoning be integrated into Transformer attention mechanisms to improve the model's ability to capture complex dependencies and generalize across tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces graph-aware attention mechanisms (GIN-Attention and Sparse-GIN-Attention) that integrate graph neural network principles into Transformers, improving relational reasoning and generalization.
papers.conclusion: Integrating graph-based reasoning into Transformers improves their performance and generalization, offering a new perspective on attention mechanisms and paving the way for more interpretable and adaptable architectures.
papers.key_findings:
GIN-Attention outperforms standard attention in training efficiency and validation performance, with reduced overfitting.
Sparse-GIN fine-tuning achieves lower validation perplexity compared to LoRA and other configurations.
The trainable sharpening parameter in GIN-Attention shows a strategic distribution across layers.
PNA-Attention did not improve upon the standard attention in the experiments conducted.
The proposed methods bridge graph theory and Transformer architectures, revealing latent graph-like structures in attention.
future_direction: Exploring the use of external adjacency matrices added to attention mechanisms.
Developing trainable methods to construct adjacency matrices that could replace or complement attention.
Exploring natural transformations for designing more robust and adaptive attention mechanisms.
papers.abstract: We present an approach to modifying Transformer architectures by integrating graph-aware relational reasoning into the attention mechanism, merging concepts from graph neural networks and language modeling. Building on the inherent connection between attention and graph theory, we reformulate the Transformer's attention mechanism as a graph operation and propose Graph-Aware Isomorphic Attention. This method leverages advanced graph modeling strategies, including Graph Isomorphism Networks (GIN) and Principal Neighborhood Aggregation (PNA), to enrich the representation of relational structures. Our approach captures complex dependencies and generalizes across tasks, as evidenced by a reduced generalization gap and improved learning performance. Additionally, we expand the concept of graph-aware attention to introduce Sparse GIN-Attention, a fine-tuning approach that employs sparse GINs. By interpreting attention matrices as sparse adjacency graphs, this technique enhances the adaptability of pre-trained foundational models with minimal computational overhead, endowing them with graph-aware capabilities. Sparse GIN-Attention fine-tuning achieves improved training dynamics and better generalization compared to alternative methods like low-rank adaption (LoRA). We discuss latent graph-like structures within traditional attention mechanisms, offering a new lens through which Transformers can be understood. By evolving Transformers as hierarchical GIN models for relational reasoning. This perspective suggests profound implications for foundational model development, enabling the design of architectures that dynamically adapt to both local and global dependencies. Applications in bioinformatics, materials science, language modeling, and beyond could benefit from this synthesis of relational and sequential data modeling, setting the stage for interpretable and generalizable modeling strategies.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: Large Language Models Encode Semantics and Alignment in Linearly Separable Representations
