papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that FFN neurons in large language models exhibit sparsity (dead neurons), act as token and n-gram detectors that explicitly suppress their triggering tokens, and encode positional information, with these properties changing with model scale.
papers.conclusion: FFN neurons in LLMs play diverse roles including dead neurons, n-gram detectors that suppress their triggers, and positional neurons, indicating that the key-value memory view of FFNs is incomplete and their roles are still poorly understood.
papers.key_findings:
Many FFN neurons are 'dead' (never activate) especially in early layers, and larger models are more sparse.
Alive neurons in early layers often act as token and n-gram detectors, with each neuron dedicated to a small set of tokens or n-grams.
Token-detecting neurons not only promote next token candidates but also suppress the triggering tokens, indicating explicit removal of current token information from the residual stream.
Some neurons are positional, activating based on token position regardless of textual content, and they often collaborate to cover position ranges.
With scale, models have more dead neurons and token detectors, and encode position less explicitly (moving away from absolute position).
papers.limitation:
Dead neurons might correspond to patterns so rare that they are not encountered in the data used.
The 350m model behaves differently due to implementation details (LayerNorm placement), showing that modeling choices affect interpretability.
future_direction: Explore mechanisms that remove information from the residual stream further.
Further understand the roles of FFN layers beyond the key-value memory view.
papers.abstract: We analyze a family of large language models in such a lightweight manner that can be done on a single GPU. Specifically, we focus on the OPT family of models ranging from 125m to 66b parameters and rely only on whether an FFN neuron is activated or not. First, we find that the early part of the network is sparse and represents many discrete features. Here, many neurons (more than 70% in some layers of the 66b model) are "dead", i.e. they never activate on a large collection of diverse data. At the same time, many of the alive neurons are reserved for discrete features and act as token and n-gram detectors. Interestingly, their corresponding FFN updates not only promote next token candidates as could be expected, but also explicitly focus on removing the information about triggering them tokens, i.e., current input. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first example of mechanisms specialized at removing (rather than adding) information from the residual stream. With scale, models become more sparse in a sense that they have more dead neurons and token detectors. Finally, some neurons are positional: them being activated or not depends largely (or solely) on position and less so (or not at all) on textual data. We find that smaller models have sets of neurons acting as position range indicators while larger models operate in a less explicit manner.

papers.title: The Confidence Manifold: Geometric Structure of Correctness Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the geometric structure of correctness representations in language models, and how can it be used for efficient detection of model errors?
papers.core_contribution: The discriminative signal for correctness in language models is low-dimensional (3-8 dimensions) and linearly separable; centroid distance in this subspace matches trained probe performance, enabling few-shot error detection.
papers.conclusion: The confidence manifold is simpler than expected, with a low-dimensional linear structure, enabling efficient geometric detection of model errors via centroid distance.
papers.key_findings:
The confidence signal occupies 3-8 dimensions, and adding more dimensions hurts performance.
The signal is linearly separable; no nonlinear classifier improves over linear probes.
Centroid distance in the low-dimensional subspace matches trained probe performance, enabling few-shot detection with minimal labels.
Internal probes achieve high AUC (0.80-0.97) while output-based methods like semantic entropy perform poorly (0.44-0.64).
Activation steering validates causality: the learned direction produces monotonic, 10.9 percentage point changes in error rates.
papers.limitation: The signal does not transfer well to tasks like HaluEval (summarization faithfulness), indicating specificity to factual QA.
papers.abstract: When a language model asserts that "the capital of Australia is Sydney," does it know this is wrong? We characterize the geometry of correctness representations across 9 models from 5 architecture families. The structure is simple: the discriminative signal occupies 3-8 dimensions, performance degrades with additional dimensions, and no nonlinear classifier improves over linear separation. Centroid distance in the low-dimensional subspace matches trained probe performance (0.90 AUC), enabling few-shot detection: on GPT-2, 25 labeled examples achieve 89% of full-data accuracy. We validate causally through activation steering: the learned direction produces 10.9 percentage point changes in error rates while random directions show no effect. Internal probes achieve 0.80-0.97 AUC; output-based methods (P(True), semantic entropy) achieve only 0.44-0.64 AUC. The correctness signal exists internally but is not expressed in outputs. That centroid distance matches probe performance indicates class separation is a mean shift, making detection geometric rather than learned.

papers.title: Quantifying LLM Attention-Head Stability: Implications for Circuit Universality
papers.research_question: Do transformers learn the same internal representations across different training runs, specifically focusing on the stability of attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically quantifies the stability of attention heads across different training runs of transformer language models, finding that middle-layer heads are least stable, weight decay improves stability, and the residual stream is more stable, with implications for circuit universality in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The findings establish that cross-instance robustness of circuits is an essential prerequisite for scalable oversight, highlighting the importance of stability in interpretability for AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
Middle-layer attention heads are the least stable across refits and the most representationally distinct.
Deeper models exhibit stronger mid-depth divergence in attention head stability.
Unstable heads in deeper layers become more functionally important than their peers.
Using AdamW optimizer with weight decay substantially improves attention-head stability across refits.
The residual stream is comparatively more stable than attention heads across refits.
papers.limitation: CKA can underestimate similarity when refits differ by transformations outside its scope, potentially affecting residual stream stability comparisons.
future_direction: Extend analysis to larger models and different architectures.
Investigate stability patterns in vision transformers or other modalities.
Explore the effect of different training regimes or data distributions on stability.
papers.abstract: In mechanistic interpretability, recent work scrutinizes transformer "circuits" - sparse, mono or multi layer sub computations, that may reflect human understandable functions. Yet, these network circuits are rarely acid-tested for their stability across different instances of the same deep learning architecture. Without this, it remains unclear whether reported circuits emerge universally across labs or turn out to be idiosyncratic to a particular estimation instance, potentially limiting confidence in safety-critical settings. Here, we systematically study stability across-refits in increasingly complex transformer language models of various sizes. We quantify, layer by layer, how similarly attention heads learn representations across independently initialized training runs. Our rigorous experiments show that (1) middle-layer heads are the least stable yet the most representationally distinct; (2) deeper models exhibit stronger mid-depth divergence; (3) unstable heads in deeper layers become more functionally important than their peers from the same layer; (4) applying weight decay optimization substantially improves attention-head stability across random model initializations; and (5) the residual stream is comparatively stable. Our findings establish the cross-instance robustness of circuits as an essential yet underappreciated prerequisite for scalable oversight, drawing contours around possible white-box monitorability of AI systems.

papers.title: Probing and Boosting Large Language Models Capabilities via Attention Heads
papers.research_question: How can we establish a correspondence between fundamental LLM capabilities and internal attention heads, and leverage this correspondence for targeted instruction tuning to improve model performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes a correspondence between fundamental LLM capabilities and internal attention heads, and leverages this correspondence for targeted instruction tuning via a lightweight, gradient-free data selection method.
papers.conclusion: The paper systematically explored the correspondence between fundamental application capabilities and attention mechanisms, revealing capability-attention head correspondence, practical effectiveness, and capability composability.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads can be used to predict specific capabilities with over 70% discrimination accuracy.
The top-16 attention heads for different capabilities show little overlap, indicating high discriminability of the capability taxonomy.
Using capability-specific attention heads for data selection improves performance on MMLU and BBH, outperforming gradient-based (LESS) and other intermediate-state baselines.
Performance improves with up to 16 concatenated attention heads but degrades with 32 heads due to increased overlap and reduced discriminability.
A certain volume of high-quality data (4-5%) is sufficient for capability enhancement; adding more mixed data can be detrimental.
papers.limitation: Experimental validation is limited to models up to 8B parameters due to computational resource constraints.
future_direction: Leverage activation patterns of capability-specific attention heads to provide interpretability for LLM outputs.
Restrict fine-tuning to only capability-specific heads for more fine-grained model adaptation.

papers.title: Pretrained Transformers as Universal Computation Engines
papers.research_question: We investigate the capability of a transformer pretrained on natural language to generalize to other modalities with minimal finetuning.
papers.core_contribution: A transformer pretrained on natural language can be effectively transferred to non-language tasks by freezing the self-attention and feedforward layers and only finetuning a small set of parameters, achieving strong performance.
papers.conclusion: Language-pretrained transformers can serve as universal computation engines, transferring effectively to non-language tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen Pretrained Transformer (FPT) achieves comparable performance to fully trained transformers on a variety of non-language tasks.
Language pretraining improves performance and compute efficiency over random initialization.
The transformer architecture (even randomly initialized) outperforms LSTM architectures on these tasks.
FPT converges faster than randomly initialized transformers.
The frozen attention layers learn to attend to semantically meaningful patterns in the data (e.g., in bit tasks).
future_direction: Investigating how to increase model expressiveness for better performance.
Exploring multimodal training/architectures.
Studying the role of different pretraining objectives and datasets.
papers.abstract: We investigate the capability of a transformer pretrained on natural language to generalize to other modalities with minimal finetuning -- in particular, without finetuning of the self-attention and feedforward layers of the residual blocks. We consider such a model, which we call a Frozen Pretrained Transformer (FPT), and study finetuning it on a variety of sequence classification tasks spanning numerical computation, vision, and protein fold prediction. In contrast to prior works which investigate finetuning on the same modality as the pretraining dataset, we show that pretraining on natural language can improve performance and compute efficiency on non-language downstream tasks. Additionally, we perform an analysis of the architecture, comparing the performance of a random initialized transformer to a random LSTM. Combining the two insights, we find language-pretrained transformers can obtain strong performance on a variety of non-language tasks.

papers.title: LyTimeT: Towards Robust and Interpretable State-Variable Discovery
papers.research_question: How to extract true dynamical variables from high-dimensional video data robustly and interpretably, despite distracting visual factors such as background motion, occlusions, and texture changes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LyTimeT, a two-phase framework that combines global spatio-temporal attention with Lyapunov-based stability regularization to learn robust, interpretable latent representations of dynamical systems from video.
papers.conclusion: LyTimeT bridges representation learning and stability theory, providing a principled foundation for robust, generalizable, and scientifically meaningful modeling of complex dynamical systems.
papers.key_findings:
LyTimeT achieves mutual information and intrinsic dimension estimates closest to ground truth compared to baselines like NSV and TIDE.
LyTimeT delivers the lowest analytical mean squared error among CNN-based and transformer-only baselines.
LyTimeT remains invariant under background perturbations, demonstrating robustness to nuisance variation.
Lyapunov regularization improves MI, lowers AMSE, and reduces long-horizon error, enhancing stability and interpretability.
LyTimeT-Lite variant maintains near-optimal performance with lower computational cost, suitable for real-time deployment.
future_direction: Incorporating physics-informed priors such as symplectic structures, conservation laws, or energy-preserving constraints.
Investigating hierarchical and sparse attention mechanisms to scale to higher-resolution videos and partially observed systems.
Exploring online or continual learning to adapt latent variables in evolving environments for closed-loop control applications.
papers.abstract: Extracting the true dynamical variables of a system from high-dimensional video is challenging due to distracting visual factors such as background motion, occlusions, and texture changes. We propose LyTimeT, a two-phase framework for interpretable variable extraction that learns robust and stable latent representations of dynamical systems. In Phase 1, LyTimeT employs a spatio-temporal TimeSformer-based autoencoder that uses global attention to focus on dynamically relevant regions while suppressing nuisance variation, enabling distraction-robust latent state learning and accurate long-horizon video prediction. In Phase 2, we probe the learned latent space, select the most physically meaningful dimensions using linear correlation analysis, and refine the transition dynamics with a Lyapunov-based stability regularizer to enforce contraction and reduce error accumulation during roll-outs. Experiments on five synthetic benchmarks and four real-world dynamical systems, including chaotic phenomena, show that LyTimeT achieves mutual information and intrinsic dimension estimates closest to ground truth, remains invariant under background perturbations, and delivers the lowest analytical mean squared error among CNN-based (TIDE) and transformer-only baselines. Our results demonstrate that combining spatio-temporal attention with stability constraints yields predictive models that are not only accurate but also physically interpretable.

papers.title: Superscopes: Amplifying Internal Feature Representations for Language Model Interpretation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret internal representations (like MLP outputs and hidden states) in language models that are not interpretable with existing self-interpretation methods, by amplifying weak features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Superscopes, a method that amplifies weak features in internal representations (MLP outputs and hidden states) to enable their interpretation via self-interpretation methods like Patchscopes, without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: Superscopes extends Patchscopes by amplifying internal representations, enabling interpretation of previously uninterpretable MLP outputs and hidden states, and draws a parallel to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models.
papers.key_findings:
Amplifying MLP outputs reveals meaningful interpretations that are not accessible with standard Patchscopes.
Amplifying hidden states can reveal interpretations in layers before contextualization occurs.
The amplification technique is analogous to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models, as both amplify directional shifts.
The Superscopes framework can automatically identify optimal amplification factors for interpretation.
The method demonstrates that weak features in internal representations can be amplified to reveal semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The method does not currently handle attention outputs, which may have a denser superposition of features.
The method for selecting the optimal amplifier may not be fully effective and could be improved.
future_direction: Extracting meaning from attention outputs.
Developing more effective approaches for selecting the optimal amplifier.
Exploring alternative ways to amplify meaning within Superscopes, such as using a different base vector for patching.
papers.abstract: Understanding and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains an open challenge. Patchscopes introduced a method for probing internal activations by patching them into new prompts, prompting models to self-explain their hidden representations. We introduce Superscopes, a technique that systematically amplifies superposed features in MLP outputs (multilayer perceptron) and hidden states before patching them into new contexts. Inspired by the "features as directions" perspective and the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) approach from diffusion models, Superscopes amplifies weak but meaningful features, enabling the interpretation of internal representations that previous methods failed to explain-all without requiring additional training. This approach provides new insights into how LLMs build context and represent complex concepts, further advancing mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Deep Hidden Cognition Facilitates Reliable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Can the model’s internal activations effectively distinguish between truthful and false branches in CoT reasoning, and can these signals be used to guide more reliable CoT decoding?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method that leverages the model's internal truthfulness sensitivity, identified via probing attention heads, to train a confidence predictor. This predictor is then used to guide beam search during CoT generation, significantly enhancing the reliability of CoT reasoning by reducing error accumulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method, which leverages internal truthfulness signals to train a confidence predictor and guide CoT generation, significantly enhances the reliability of CoT reasoning across diverse tasks and models.
papers.key_findings:
The model's internal activations during CoT reasoning encode truthfulness information, which can be extracted via probing attention heads.
A confidence predictor trained on these activations outperforms baselines like sequence likelihood and verbalized confidence in calibration metrics.
Integrating the confidence predictor into a beam search framework for CoT generation improves reasoning accuracy across diverse unimodal and multimodal tasks and model scales.
The method is compatible with self-correction techniques and generalizes to specialized reasoning models like DeepSeek R1.
papers.abstract: Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning has demonstrated remarkable deep reasoning capabilities in both large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, its reliability is often undermined by the accumulation of errors in intermediate steps. This paper introduces an novel approach to calibrate the CoT reasoning accuracy by leveraging the model's intrinsic veracity encoding. We discover that specific attention head activations reliably reflect the truthfulness of reasoning steps in CoT. Based on this insight, we train a confidence predictor to evaluate the correctness of each reasoning step using these truthfulness-sensitive activations, dynamically selecting the most plausible reasoning path via beam search. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines (e.g., Few-Shot CoT, Self-Consistency, and Self-Evaluation Guided Beam Search) across the mathematical, symbolic, and commonsense reasoning tasks, exhibiting superior accuracy and reliability in both unimodal and multimodal settings. We further validate the approach on large reasoning models, confirming its applicability to specialized reasoning models. Additionally, we explore the role of the model's self-correction ability in CoT reasoning. This work provides a novel reliability improvement path for CoT reasoning with broad application potential.

papers.title: Interpreting Language Models Through Concept Descriptions: A Survey
papers.research_question: The paper surveys the field of concept descriptions for model components, aiming to answer questions about common methods and data sources, best practices for evaluation, observed trends, and key gaps and future directions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions, charting methods, evaluation techniques, and datasets, and identifies a growing demand for rigorous causal evaluation and provides a roadmap for future research.
papers.conclusion: The use of LLMs to generate concept descriptions is a notable step towards demystifying LLMs, with a trajectory from labeling neurons to abstractions and maturing evaluation methods, but the path to verifiable causal mechanisms is not yet fully paved and costs and faithfulness concerns remain.
papers.key_findings:
Recognition of neuron polysemanticity has driven adoption of model abstractions like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and frameworks for multiple concepts per feature.
Evaluation of concept descriptions is maturing, with multi-faceted metrics assessing predictive power, input accuracy, and causal faithfulness.
The field is moving from labeling individual neurons to higher-level abstractions like SAEs and circuits.
There is a need for more rigorous causal evaluation and standardized benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Focus limited to natural language concept descriptions for internal model components and abstractions, excluding other interpretability work.
Substantial computational and financial costs associated with the methods surveyed.
Focus on English-language models and text corpora, with generalization to other languages being an open question.
future_direction: Scaling automated description methods to circuits.
Applying concept description methods to new data domains and modalities.
Analyzing the interpreters (LLMs) themselves to understand biases and limitations in generated descriptions.
papers.abstract: Understanding the decision-making processes of neural networks is a central goal of mechanistic interpretability. In the context of Large Language Models (LLMs), this involves uncovering the underlying mechanisms and identifying the roles of individual model components such as neurons and attention heads, as well as model abstractions such as the learned sparse features extracted by Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). A rapidly growing line of work tackles this challenge by using powerful generator models to produce open-vocabulary, natural language concept descriptions for these components. In this paper, we provide the first survey of the emerging field of concept descriptions for model components and abstractions. We chart the key methods for generating these descriptions, the evolving landscape of automated and human metrics for evaluating them, and the datasets that underpin this research. Our synthesis reveals a growing demand for more rigorous, causal evaluation. By outlining the state of the art and identifying key challenges, this survey provides a roadmap for future research toward making models more transparent.

papers.title: Mapping Clinical Doubt: Locating Linguistic Uncertainty in LLMs
papers.research_question: How are epistemic signals encoding linguistic uncertainty represented across the layers of LLMs, and are these representations stable across model variants?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Model Sensitivity to Uncertainty (MSU), a layer-wise probing metric, and demonstrates that LLMs encode linguistic uncertainty progressively in deeper layers, with sensitivity increasing monotonically with depth.
papers.conclusion: Encoding of epistemic uncertainty is a distributed and emergent property in transformer architectures, peaking in final layers, and the MSU metric provides a targeted lens for interpretability and epistemic awareness.
papers.key_findings:
MSU scores increase monotonically with depth across all tested models, indicating greater sensitivity to epistemic uncertainty in later layers.
PCA reveals clustering and geometric inversion in deeper layers, suggesting semantic reorganization of uncertainty representations.
Later layers exhibit substantially higher sensitivity to epistemic modals, aligning with their role in encoding abstract semantics.
The pattern of late-emerging sensitivity is consistent across different model families and instruction-tuning variants.
Uncertainty is treated as a high-level semantic feature that is progressively amplified across the transformer stack.
papers.limitation: Findings are based on a limited set of instruction-tuned models, so their generality across architectures, sizes, and pretraining paradigms remains uncertain.
future_direction: Expand to diverse model types, including non-instruct, multilingual, and domain-specific models.
Localize uncertainty to specific neurons or attention heads.
Examine how internal uncertainty signals (e.g., logits, entropy) relate to output confidence and calibration.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in clinical settings, where sensitivity to linguistic uncertainty can influence diagnostic interpretation and decision-making. Yet little is known about where such epistemic cues are internally represented within these models. Distinct from uncertainty quantification, which measures output confidence, this work examines input-side representational sensitivity to linguistic uncertainty in medical text. We curate a contrastive dataset of clinical statements varying in epistemic modality (e.g., 'is consistent with' vs. 'may be consistent with') and propose Model Sensitivity to Uncertainty (MSU), a layerwise probing metric that quantifies activation-level shifts induced by uncertainty cues. Our results show that LLMs exhibit structured, depth-dependent sensitivity to clinical uncertainty, suggesting that epistemic information is progressively encoded in deeper layers. These findings reveal how linguistic uncertainty is internally represented in LLMs, offering insight into their interpretability and epistemic reliability.

papers.title: Unveiling Simplicities of Attention: Adaptive Long-Context Head Identification
papers.research_question: Can we identify which attention heads require long-context information to predict the next token accurately, and how much sparsity can we gain using query-adaptive criteria compared to static criteria?
papers.core_contribution: It is possible to predict which attention heads are crucial for long-context processing using only local keys and a Gaussian approximation of the key distribution, and query-adaptive criteria can achieve higher sparsity than static criteria without sacrificing performance.
papers.conclusion: Attention heads exhibit query-dependent behavior (local vs long-context), and a simple test based on second-order statistics (QAdA) can effectively predict this behavior, enabling significant efficiency gains in long-context processing.
papers.key_findings:
Static criteria can label up to 60% of heads as local without performance drop, but a query-adaptive oracle can label up to 90%.
The proposed QAdA method efficiently identifies long-context heads using second-order statistics of keys, achieving near-oracle performance with lower computational cost.
QAdA outperforms static criteria on various long-context benchmarks and models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen).
Attention head behavior (local vs long-context) is query-dependent and varies across layers and tasks.
Using moment statistics from a random words prompt (unrelated to the current prompt) yields robust performance for QAdA.
papers.limitation: The paper does not test and provide a highly optimized implementation compatible with flash attention, and does not showcase real run-time gains.
papers.abstract: The ability to process long contexts is crucial for many natural language processing tasks, yet it remains a significant challenge. While substantial progress has been made in enhancing the efficiency of attention mechanisms, there is still a gap in understanding how attention heads function in long-context settings. In this paper, we observe that while certain heads consistently attend to local information only, others swing between attending to local and long-context information depending on the query. This raises the question: can we identify which heads require long-context information to predict the next token accurately? We demonstrate that it's possible to predict which heads are crucial for long-context processing using only local keys. The core idea here is to exploit a simple model for the long-context scores via second moment approximations. These findings unveil simple properties of attention in the context of long sequences, and open the door to potentially significant gains in efficiency.

papers.title: Emergent Semantics Beyond Token Embeddings: Transformer LMs with Frozen Visual Unicode Representations
papers.research_question: Can semantic understanding in Transformer language models emerge without trainable, semantically-rich input embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs with frozen, non-semantic visual Unicode embeddings can learn semantic understanding and outperform identical models with trainable embeddings on reasoning benchmarks, indicating semantics are an emergent property of the architecture, not the input embeddings.
papers.conclusion: Semantics in neural language models is not a property of the embedding matrix but an emergent phenomenon of the model's layered composition and self-attention, opening new avenues for model standardization, modularity, and efficient scaling.
papers.key_findings:
Models with frozen visual Unicode embeddings converge, generate coherent text, and outperform architecturally identical models with trainable embeddings on the MMLU reasoning benchmark.
Semantic clustering emerges in the deeper transformer layers, not in the input embeddings, as shown by t-SNE visualizations.
Even randomly initialized frozen embeddings allow the model to converge, suggesting semantic structures in trainable embeddings are an emergent artifact, not a prerequisite.
The 'representational interference' hypothesis posits that trainable embeddings are burdened with learning both structural and semantic features, leading to suboptimal performance.
Frozen embeddings provide a stable structural foundation, freeing the transformer's attention and feed-forward layers to focus on composing these primitives into high-level meaning.
papers.limitation:
The study was intentionally constrained in scale (0.3B parameters, 4B tokens); future work should test whether findings hold for models at the 10B+ parameter scale.
Generalization to truly novel modalities (e.g., mathematical formulas, chemical structures) remains an open question.
future_direction: Test whether these findings hold for models at the 10B+ parameter scale.
Explore the method's generalization to novel modalities (e.g., mathematical formulas, chemical structures).
Investigate applications in modular and standardized embeddings, efficient Mixture-of-Experts, and cross-lingual transfer.
papers.abstract: Understanding the locus of semantic representation in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for interpretability and architectural innovation. The dominant paradigm posits that trainable input embeddings serve as foundational "meaning vectors." This paper challenges that view. We construct Transformer models where the embedding layer is entirely frozen, with vectors derived not from data, but from the visual structure of Unicode glyphs. These non-semantic, precomputed visual embeddings are fixed throughout training. Our method is compatible with any tokenizer, including a novel Unicode-centric tokenizer we introduce to ensure universal text coverage. Despite the absence of trainable, semantically initialized embeddings, our models converge, generate coherent text, and, critically, outperform architecturally identical models with trainable embeddings on the MMLU reasoning benchmark. We attribute this to "representational interference" in conventional models, where the embedding layer is burdened with learning both structural and semantic features. Our results indicate that high-level semantics are not inherent to input embeddings but are an emergent property of the Transformer's compositional architecture and data scale. This reframes the role of embeddings from meaning containers to structural primitives. We release all code and models to foster further research.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: MolEdit: Knowledge Editing for Multimodal Molecule Language Models
papers.research_question: How to edit knowledge in multimodal molecule language models (MoLMs) to correct inaccuracies while preserving unrelated knowledge, specifically for molecule-to-caption and caption-to-molecule generation tasks.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MolEdit, a framework for editing multimodal molecule language models, and MEBench, a benchmark for evaluating such editing, addressing molecule-specific challenges of multifaceted expertise and cross-molecule interdependence.
papers.conclusion: MolEdit provides an effective framework for editing multimodal molecule language models, enabling precise knowledge updates while preserving unrelated information, and MEBench offers a comprehensive evaluation benchmark, charting a path toward safer, continuously updatable scientific foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
MolEdit outperforms fine-tuning, gradient-based (MEND), and memory-based (GRACE) baselines across Reliability, Locality, and Generality metrics on both MoMu and MolFM backbones.
MolEdit achieves up to 18.8% higher Reliability and 12.0% better Locality than state-of-the-art editing baselines.
Editing molecule generation is more challenging than editing caption generation, and performance is generally better on MoMu than on MolFM.
The Multi-Expert Knowledge Adapter (MEKA) effectively routes different facets of molecular knowledge to specialized experts, and the Expertise-Aware Editing Switcher (EAES) accurately activates edits only for relevant inputs.
Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component (MEKA and EAES) to MolEdit's overall performance.
papers.limitation:
Editing molecular SMILES strings is inherently more complex and abstract than editing captions, lacking explicit semantic structure.
Potential misuse of editing to amplify unsafe molecular knowledge and inadvertent propagation of dataset biases.
future_direction: Future work on editing MoLMs.
papers.abstract: Understanding and continuously refining multimodal molecular knowledge is crucial for advancing biomedicine, chemistry, and materials science. Molecule language models (MoLMs) have become powerful tools in these domains, integrating structural representations (e.g., SMILES strings, molecular graphs) with rich contextual descriptions (e.g., physicochemical properties). However, MoLMs can encode and propagate inaccuracies due to outdated web-mined training corpora or malicious manipulation, jeopardizing downstream discovery pipelines. While knowledge editing has been explored for general-domain AI, its application to MoLMs remains uncharted, presenting unique challenges due to the multifaceted and interdependent nature of molecular knowledge. In this paper, we take the first step toward MoLM editing for two critical tasks: molecule-to-caption generation and caption-to-molecule generation. To address molecule-specific challenges, we propose MolEdit, a powerful framework that enables targeted modifications while preserving unrelated molecular knowledge. MolEdit combines a Multi-Expert Knowledge Adapter that routes edits to specialized experts for different molecular facets with an Expertise-Aware Editing Switcher that activates the adapters only when input closely matches the stored edits across all expertise, minimizing interference with unrelated knowledge. To systematically evaluate editing performance, we introduce MEBench, a comprehensive benchmark assessing multiple dimensions, including Reliability (accuracy of the editing), Locality (preservation of irrelevant knowledge), and Generality (robustness to reformed queries). Across extensive experiments on two popular MoLM backbones, MolEdit delivers up to 18.8% higher Reliability and 12.0% better Locality than baselines while maintaining efficiency. The code is available at: https://github.com/LzyFischer/MolEdit.

papers.title: Explaining reaction coordinates of alanine dipeptide isomerization obtained from deep neural networks using Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)
papers.research_question: How can Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods explain which collective variables contribute to the reaction coordinates predicted by deep neural networks for alanine dipeptide isomerization?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that XAI methods (LIME and SHAP) can provide local explanations for the contribution of collective variables to reaction coordinates predicted by a deep neural network for alanine dipeptide isomerization, revealing the importance of specific dihedral angles.
papers.conclusion: The proposed AI-aided method combined with XAI provides a practical tool for locally explaining appropriate reaction coordinates from DNN training, especially near the transition state, and is applicable to complex molecular systems.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks can be trained to predict appropriate reaction coordinates for alanine dipeptide isomerization.
Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation (LIME) and Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provide local explanations of feature contributions to the predicted reaction coordinates.
Near the transition state, the dihedral angle θ becomes more important than near the stable states, indicating its role in crossing the barrier.
The feature contributions from LIME and SHAP are consistent, justifying LIME's linear model assumption.
The method can identify dominant collective variables consistent with previous committor test analyses.
papers.limitation: Understanding the detailed mechanism for complex molecular systems becomes complicated because of the large numbers of collective variables.
future_direction: Application to solute-solvent systems such as alanine dipeptide in explicit water.
Application to various other solute-solvent systems.
papers.abstract: A method for obtaining appropriate reaction coordinates is required to identify transition states distinguishing the product and reactant in complex molecular systems. Recently, abundant research has been devoted to obtaining reaction coordinates using artificial neural networks from deep learning literature, where many collective variables are typically utilized in the input layer. However, it is difficult to explain the details of which collective variables contribute to the predicted reaction coordinates owing to the complexity of the nonlinear functions in deep neural networks. To overcome this limitation, we used Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods of the Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanation (LIME) and the game theory-based framework known as Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). We demonstrated that XAI enables us to obtain the degree of contribution of each collective variable to reaction coordinates that is determined by nonlinear regressions with deep learning for the committor of the alanine dipeptide isomerization in vacuum. In particular, both LIME and SHAP provide important features to the predicted reaction coordinates, which are characterized by appropriate dihedral angles consistent with those previously reported from the committor test analysis. The present study offers an AI-aided framework to explain the appropriate reaction coordinates, which acquires considerable significance when the number of degrees of freedom increases.

papers.title: FuxiTranyu: A Multilingual Large Language Model Trained with Balanced Data
papers.research_question: How to build a multilingual large language model with balanced data to mitigate performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FuxiTranyu, a multilingual LLM trained on balanced data, which shows competitive performance and more consistent multilingual representations compared to existing models.
papers.conclusion: FuxiTranyu is a strong open-source multilingual LLM, and balanced pre-training data is crucial for achieving consistent multilingual representations and performance.
papers.key_findings:
FuxiTranyu outperforms previous multilingual LLMs like BLOOM-7B1 and PolyLM-13B on several multilingual benchmarks.
Balanced pre-training data leads to more consistent multilingual representations across languages.
Neuron analysis reveals that deep layers are more language-specific and the importance of attention and MLP components varies across layers.
Languages with extremely limited resources (e.g., Bengali, Tamil) are allocated fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model achieves high performance on summarization tasks, outperforming baseline models on XL-Sum.
papers.limitation:
Languages with extremely limited resources, such as Bengali and Tamil, are allocated with fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model underperforms in some tasks (e.g., m-ARC, m-MMLU) due to limited training data for English.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated prowess in a wide range of tasks. However, many LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages. To mitigate this challenge, we present FuxiTranyu, an open-source multilingual LLM, which is designed to satisfy the need of the research community for balanced and high-performing multilingual capabilities. The base model, FuxiTranyu-8B, features 8 billion parameters and is trained from scratch on meticulously balanced multilingual data that contains 600 billion tokens covering 43 natural languages and 16 programming languages. We also develop two instruction-tuned models: FuxiTranyu-8B-SFT which is fine-tuned on a diverse multilingual instruction dataset, and FuxiTranyu-8B-DPO which is further refined with DPO on a preference dataset for enhanced alignment ability. Extensive experiments on a wide range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate the competitive performance of FuxiTranyu against existing multilingual LLMs, e.g., BLOOM-7B, PolyLM-13B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Both neuron and representation interpretability analyses reveal that FuxiTranyu achieves consistent multilingual representations across languages. To promote further research into multilingual LLMs, we release both the base and instruction-tuned FuxiTranyu models together with 58 pre-training checkpoints at HuggingFace (see https://huggingface.co/TJUNLP/FuxiTranyu-8B) and Github (see https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/FuxiTranyu).

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Presents evidence that induction heads, a type of attention head circuit, are the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads likely explain a large fraction of in-context learning in transformers, with strong evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form abruptly during a phase change in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in in-context learning ability.
Altering the transformer architecture to shift the formation of induction heads also shifts the improvement in in-context learning.
Ablating induction heads in small models greatly reduces in-context learning.
Induction heads exhibit general in-context learning behaviors beyond literal copying, such as translation.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models suggests how they could be repurposed for general in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Evidence for large models is correlational and could be confounded by other factors.
future_direction: Establish the claim more firmly with additional evidence
Study the phase change in more detail
papers.abstract: "Induction heads" are attention heads that implement a simple algorithm to complete token sequences like [A][B] ... [A] -> [B]. In this work, we present preliminary and indirect evidence for a hypothesis that induction heads might constitute the mechanism for the majority of all "in-context learning" in large transformer models (i.e. decreasing loss at increasing token indices). We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: Do Long-Range Language Models Actually Use Long-Range Context?
papers.research_question: How do long-range Transformer language models use long-range context? Do they encode important discourse information to improve their predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Long-range Transformer language models rarely exploit long-range context meaningfully; improvements are superficial, such as copying tokens from distant context.
papers.conclusion: Long-range Transformer language models do not meaningfully use long-range context; future research should include analysis experiments to understand context usage.
papers.key_findings:
Providing long-range context beyond 2K tokens only improves predictions on a small set of tokens, like infrequent tokens or those that can be copied from distant context.
Perturbing the long-range context with shuffling or random replacement has minimal impact on overall perplexity, suggesting models encode context superficially.
Long-range context does not help for sequence-level prediction tasks like suffix identification, indicating limited use beyond token-level teacher-forcing.
The benefits of long-range context vary by book type, helping most for literary novels as opposed to textbooks or magazines.
Models encode token identity in distant context to some extent but do not capture complex discourse structure or word order.
papers.limitation:
An artifact in the Routing Transformer causes tokens at the very end of a sequence to have much higher losses, affecting evaluation.
Evaluating every token in the validation set with large prefix sizes is computationally infeasible, limiting the scope of analysis.
Other long-range LMs like Compressive Transformer and Longformer could not be analyzed due to lack of publicly-available checkpoints.
future_direction: Future research on long-range LMs should include analysis experiments to shed light on how and when they use distant context.
papers.abstract: Language models are generally trained on short, truncated input sequences, which limits their ability to use discourse-level information present in long-range context to improve their predictions. Recent efforts to improve the efficiency of self-attention have led to a proliferation of long-range Transformer language models, which can process much longer sequences than models of the past. However, the ways in which such models take advantage of the long-range context remain unclear. In this paper, we perform a fine-grained analysis of two long-range Transformer language models (including the \emph{Routing Transformer}, which achieves state-of-the-art perplexity on the PG-19 long-sequence LM benchmark dataset) that accept input sequences of up to 8K tokens. Our results reveal that providing long-range context (i.e., beyond the previous 2K tokens) to these models only improves their predictions on a small set of tokens (e.g., those that can be copied from the distant context) and does not help at all for sentence-level prediction tasks. Finally, we discover that PG-19 contains a variety of different document types and domains, and that long-range context helps most for literary novels (as opposed to textbooks or magazines).

papers.title: Controllability Analysis of State Space-based Language Model
papers.research_question: Can the Influence Score, a controllability measure derived from control theory, serve as a diagnostic tool for interpreting, comparing, and understanding the internal dynamics of SSM-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper validates the Influence Score, a novel controllability measure derived from Mamba's state-space parameters, as a diagnostic tool for SSM-based language models, revealing scaling effects, architectural signatures, and emergent behaviors related to model capacity and robustness.
papers.conclusion: The Influence Score is a promising diagnostic tool for interpreting, comparing, and understanding the internal dynamics of SSM-based language models, revealing core architectural properties and emergent behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
The Influence Score scales directly with model size and training data quality, serving as a proxy for model capacity.
Mamba exhibits consistent architectural signatures: a strong recency bias (position sensitivity) and a heavy concentration of influence in mid-to-late layers.
Emergent behaviors appear at scale: the largest model (mamba-2.8b-slimpj) intuitively ranks content words as more influential than function words and demonstrates robustness by decreasing internal influence when processing noisy inputs.
The Influence Score is largely insensitive to sampling temperature but increases systematically with prompt complexity.
The metric reveals a functional specialization across layers, with late layers showing significantly higher influence than early layers.
papers.limitation:
The Influence Score is an aggregated metric; future work should trace the influence of individual tokens or concepts through the network on a layer-by-layer basis.
The study was limited to three models; applying the framework to a wider range of SSMs and comparing to Transformers would be beneficial.
future_direction: Tracing the influence of individual tokens or concepts through the network on a layer-by-layer basis.
Applying the framework to a wider range of SSMs and comparing their influence fingerprints to traditional Transformers.
Using the Influence Score for guided generation, e.g., penalizing decoding paths that lead to unstable spikes in influence to improve model reliability.
papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs), particularly Mamba, have become powerful architectures for sequence modeling, yet their internal dynamics remain poorly understood compared to attention-based models. We introduce and validate the Influence Score, a controllability-based metric derived from the discretized state-space parameters of Mamba and computed through a backward recurrence analogous to system observability. The score quantifies how strongly a token at position k affects all later states and outputs. We evaluate this measure across three Mamba variants: mamba-130m, mamba-2.8b, and mamba-2.8b-slimpj, using six experiments that test its sensitivity to temperature, prompt complexity, token type, layer depth, token position, and input perturbations. The results show three main insights: (1) the Influence Score increases with model size and training data, reflecting model capacity; (2) Mamba exhibits consistent architectural patterns, including recency bias and concentrated influence in mid-to-late layers; and (3) emergent behaviors appear only at scale, with mamba-2.8b-slimpj uniquely prioritizing content words and reducing internal influence in the presence of noise. These findings establish the Influence Score as a practical diagnostic tool for interpreting and comparing SSM-based language models.

papers.title: Placing language in an integrated understanding system: Next steps toward human-level performance in neural language models
papers.research_question: What is the role of language in human intelligence and how can we extend current machine language models to achieve human-level language understanding by integrating language with other modalities and memory systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a framework for building an integrated understanding system that combines insights from cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence, using query-based attention and memory systems to extend current language models toward human-level language understanding.
papers.conclusion: Combining insights from neuroscience and AI will take us closer to human-level language understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Current language models are limited by their focus on language-internal tasks and lack of memory for remote information.
The human brain integrates language with other modalities and uses complementary learning systems (neocortex and medial temporal lobe) for understanding.
Query-based attention is a key innovation that can be extended to integrate multiple modalities and memory.
Future models should incorporate an MTL-like memory to handle remote information and improve data efficiency.
Understanding should be seen as constructing situation representations, which are compositional and grounded in multi-sensory experience.
papers.limitation: The proposed sketch leaves important issues open and will require substantial development.
future_direction: Incorporating an MTL-like memory to allow the use of remote information beyond the current episode.
Integrating a frontal lobe-like subsystem to guide processing according to task demands.
Extending the approach beyond concrete situations to abstract ones involving laws, belief systems, and scientific theories.
papers.abstract: Language is crucial for human intelligence, but what exactly is its role? We take language to be a part of a system for understanding and communicating about situations. In humans, these abilities emerge gradually from experience and depend on domain-general principles of biological neural networks: connection-based learning, distributed representation, and context-sensitive, mutual constraint satisfaction-based processing. Current artificial language processing systems rely on the same domain general principles, embodied in artificial neural networks. Indeed, recent progress in this field depends on query-based attention, which extends the ability of these systems to exploit context and has contributed to remarkable breakthroughs. Nevertheless, most current models focus exclusively on language-internal tasks, limiting their ability to perform tasks that depend on understanding situations. These systems also lack memory for the contents of prior situations outside of a fixed contextual span. We describe the organization of the brain's distributed understanding system, which includes a fast learning system that addresses the memory problem. We sketch a framework for future models of understanding drawing equally on cognitive neuroscience and artificial intelligence and exploiting query-based attention. We highlight relevant current directions and consider further developments needed to fully capture human-level language understanding in a computational system.

papers.title: To Sink or Not to Sink: Visual Information Pathways in Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental benefits of ViT attention sink tokens in large vision-language models, and how can they be understood and operationalized to improve visual reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes ViT attention sinks in LVLMs, finding they encode high-level semantic context, and introduces DIYSink, a framework that dynamically leverages these sinks to improve visual reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: ViT attention sinks are important carriers of high-level visual context and can be effectively leveraged, both via training-free and training-based methods, to enhance the visual reasoning capabilities of large vision-language models.
papers.key_findings:
ViT sink tokens propagate into the LLM, activating distinct hidden dimensions different from LLM-emerged sinks.
ViT sinks capture coarse-grained, high-level contextual features and are semantically meaningful.
ViT sinks are beneficial for global tasks requiring high-level understanding but can degrade performance on local, detail-rich tasks.
A simple training-free approach (sink-to-the-front) improves performance across various LVLMs.
The proposed DIYSink framework, with dual MLP projectors and dynamic token selection, yields substantial improvements across a range of benchmarks.
papers.limitation: The proposed DIYSink framework requires access to training data and computational resources for training from scratch.
future_direction: Extending DIYSink to other modalities such as video and audio.
papers.abstract: Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs) have recently emerged as powerful architectures capable of understanding and reasoning over both visual and textual information. These models typically rely on two key components: a Vision Transformer (ViT) and a Large Language Model (LLM). ViT encodes visual content into a sequence of image tokens and serves as the perceptual front-end -- the eyes of the model. In contrast, the LLM interprets these tokens to perform high-level reasoning, generates responses, and functions as the cognitive core -- the brain of the model. However, it remains unclear which visual tokens contribute most significantly to understanding and reasoning, and how effectively these signals are propagated from ViT to the LLM. While most existing works have focused on identifying attention sinks, low-semantic tokens receiving disproportionately high attention, within the LLM, we shift the focus to the vision encoder by identifying a class of high-norm visual tokens from ViT, referred to as ViT attention sinks -- a problem that has been rarely studied but is indeed very important for LVLMs. Our findings show that these ViT sinks encapsulate high-level semantic concepts from images, allowing the LLM to perform more effective understanding and reasoning. Despite their importance, these sink tokens are often overlooked in existing LVLM architectures. To explore their contribution, we present both qualitative and quantitative analyses of the information embedded in these sink tokens. We also propose both training-free and training-based approaches to better leverage how this information is interpreted by the LLM, and to what extent. By explicitly utilizing these tokens, we demonstrate substantial improvements across a range of LVLMs and visual reasoning tasks, highlighting the untapped potential of ViT attention sinks in enhancing visual reasoning.

papers.title: Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment
papers.research_question: When, why, and how does fine-tuning language models on narrow incorrect datasets lead to broad, undesirable misalignment (emergent misalignment), and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Emergent misalignment occurs across diverse fine-tuning and reinforcement learning settings and is mediated by 'misaligned persona' features in activation space, which can be used to detect, steer, and mitigate the behavior.
papers.conclusion: Emergent misalignment is a robust phenomenon that can arise from various training procedures, and interpretability methods like model-diffing with sparse autoencoders can reveal its mechanistic basis and enable detection and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Emergent misalignment occurs from supervised fine-tuning on narrow incorrect advice in diverse domains and from reinforcement learning that rewards incorrect responses.
A 'toxic persona' feature (and other related features) identified via sparse autoencoder model-diffing causally controls emergent misalignment and can be used to steer model behavior.
Fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on a few hundred benign samples efficiently re-aligns the model.
The activation level of the 'toxic persona' feature can discriminate between aligned and misaligned models, serving as a potential early-warning signal.
Emergent misalignment generally increases with model size for models capable of coherent responses.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning on natural human-generated data produces high incoherence and correlated misalignment, which may be a different effect from the emergent misalignment observed with synthetic data.
future_direction: Further work to understand training dynamics, especially the effects of off-policy fine-tuning on human data.
papers.abstract: Understanding how language models generalize behaviors from their training to a broader deployment distribution is an important problem in AI safety. Betley et al. discovered that fine-tuning GPT-4o on intentionally insecure code causes "emergent misalignment," where models give stereotypically malicious responses to unrelated prompts. We extend this work, demonstrating emergent misalignment across diverse conditions, including reinforcement learning on reasoning models, fine-tuning on various synthetic datasets, and in models without safety training. To investigate the mechanisms behind this generalized misalignment, we apply a "model diffing" approach using sparse autoencoders to compare internal model representations before and after fine-tuning. This approach reveals several "misaligned persona" features in activation space, including a toxic persona feature which most strongly controls emergent misalignment and can be used to predict whether a model will exhibit such behavior. Additionally, we investigate mitigation strategies, discovering that fine-tuning an emergently misaligned model on just a few hundred benign samples efficiently restores alignment.

papers.title: Uncovering the Computational Roles of Nonlinearity in Sequence Modeling Using Almost-Linear RNNs
papers.research_question: When is nonlinearity truly required in recurrent networks for sequence modeling, and what computational mechanisms does it enable?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Almost-Linear RNN (AL-RNN) framework to systematically dissect the functional role of nonlinearity in recurrent networks, showing that sparse nonlinearity can match or exceed the performance of fully nonlinear models while improving interpretability and efficiency.
papers.conclusion: The AL-RNN framework provides a principled approach for identifying where nonlinearity is functionally necessary in sequence models, guiding the design of recurrent architectures that balance performance, efficiency, and mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse nonlinearity improves interpretability by reducing and localizing nonlinear computations.
In multi-task settings, sparse nonlinearity promotes shared representations across tasks.
Sparse nonlinearity reduces computational cost by limiting nonlinear operations.
In low-data regimes or tasks requiring discrete switching between linear regimes, sparsely nonlinear models often match or exceed the performance of fully nonlinear architectures.
The AL-RNN framework reveals computational primitives such as gating, rule-based integration, and memory-dependent transients embedded within predominantly linear dynamical backbones.
papers.abstract: Sequence modeling tasks across domains such as natural language processing, time series forecasting, and control require learning complex input-output mappings. Nonlinear recurrence is theoretically required for universal approximation of sequence-to-sequence functions, yet linear recurrent models often prove surprisingly effective. This raises the question of when nonlinearity is truly required. We present a framework to systematically dissect the functional role of nonlinearity in recurrent networks, identifying when it is computationally necessary and what mechanisms it enables. We address this using Almost Linear Recurrent Neural Networks (AL-RNNs), which allow recurrence nonlinearity to be gradually attenuated and decompose network dynamics into analyzable linear regimes, making computational mechanisms explicit. We illustrate the framework across diverse synthetic and real-world tasks, including classic sequence modeling benchmarks, a neuroscientific stimulus-selection task, and a multi-task suite. We demonstrate how the AL-RNN's piecewise linear structure enables identification of computational primitives such as gating, rule-based integration, and memory-dependent transients, revealing that these operations emerge within predominantly linear backbones. Across tasks, sparse nonlinearity improves interpretability by reducing and localizing nonlinear computations, promotes shared representations in multi-task settings, and reduces computational cost. Moreover, sparse nonlinearity acts as a useful inductive bias: in low-data regimes or when tasks require discrete switching between linear regimes, sparsely nonlinear models often match or exceed fully nonlinear architectures. Our findings provide a principled approach for identifying where nonlinearity is functionally necessary, guiding the design of recurrent architectures that balance performance, efficiency, and interpretability.

papers.title: Peering inside the black box by learning the relevance of many-body functions in neural network potentials
papers.research_question: How can neural network potentials (NNPs), specifically coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks, be interpreted by decomposing their inferred energy into n-body interactions to provide human-understandable explanations without compromising predictive power?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends GNN-LRP (Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for Graph Neural Networks) to interpret neural network potentials for coarse-grained molecular systems, demonstrating that the decomposed n-body interactions are physically meaningful and consistent across different GNN architectures, thereby enhancing trust in these models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed GNN-LRP method successfully interprets neural network potentials by revealing physically sound many-body interactions, providing a strong argument for trusting and wider adoption of these seemingly black-box models in molecular simulations.
papers.key_findings:
GNN-LRP can decompose the energy output of a neural network potential into interpretable n-body (e.g., 2-body and 3-body) interaction contributions.
For coarse-grained methane, 3-body interactions are negligible, while for water they are significant, aligning with fundamental physical knowledge.
Different GNN architectures (PaiNN and SO3Net) trained on the same data learn similar underlying physical interactions, as revealed by their relevance attributions.
GNN-LRP can uncover subtle model artifacts in learned interactions that are not detectable through standard molecular dynamics simulation metrics.
Applied to a coarse-grained protein model (NTL9), GNN-LRP identifies stabilizing and destabilizing residue interactions in different metastable states and correctly interprets the effects of mutations.
papers.limitation: Future work is needed to refine these concepts to provide greater insight into ML models and allow researchers to be more systematic in their choice of architecture and functionalization.
future_direction: Apply the interpretation techniques to extract new scientific knowledge on previously unknown systems.
Refine the GNN-LRP concepts to provide greater insight and allow more systematic choices of architecture and functionalization.
papers.abstract: Machine learned potentials based on artificial neural networks are becoming a popular tool to define an effective energy model for complex systems, either incorporating electronic structure effects at the atomistic resolution, or effectively renormalizing part of the atomistic degrees of freedom at a coarse-grained resolution. One main criticism regarding neural network potentials is that their inferred energy is less interpretable than in traditional approaches, which use simpler and more transparent functional forms. Here we address this problem by extending tools recently proposed in the nascent field of explainable artificial intelligence to coarse-grained potentials based on graph neural networks. With these tools, neural network potentials can be practically decomposed into n-body interactions, providing a human understandable interpretation without compromising predictive power. We demonstrate the approach on three different coarse-grained systems including two fluids (methane and water) and the protein NTL9. The obtained interpretations suggest that well-trained neural network potentials learn physical interactions, which are consistent with fundamental principles.

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that input perturbations reveal how transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and that such perturbations are a useful analysis tool for interpreting deep language models.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and attention changes partially explain this sensitivity.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing context scale along layers.
Swapping phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrases, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, especially in deeper layers.
Attention changes partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance.
The distortion metric correlates with impairment of syntactic probes (POS, grandparent tags, tree distance).
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features.
Searching for causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance.
Applying perturbation analyses to models trained on shuffled data or models with explicit syntax.
papers.abstract: While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations, nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure. Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for interpreting complex black-box models. 1

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
